The dossier examines whether NuScale can convert regulatory primacy and a rebuilt balance sheet into the first closed commercial SMR contract before lower-cost competitors in China, Canada, and the United Kingdom reduce its first-mover premium.

chapters.title: Strategic Snapshot: The First-Mover Premium and Its Limits
chapters.body:
In the first quarter of 2026, NuScale Power Corporation reported $0.6 million in revenue. The number is almost too small to parse against a company carrying a market capitalization of approximately $4.5 billion — a ratio that implies investors are paying roughly $7,500 for every dollar of quarterly income the business actually generates. That arithmetic is not a valuation error. It is a precise expression of what NuScale has sold the market: not a power company, but an option on the possibility that the United States will build small modular reactors at industrial scale, and that NuScale will be the only licensed technology platform available when that moment arrives.

The option has real underlying value. NuScale holds two Nuclear Regulatory Commission design approvals that no other American SMR developer has matched — a 50 MWe Design Certification issued in January 2023 and, ahead of schedule, a 77 MWe Standard Design Approval granted in May 2025. The second approval, which governs the VOYGR-4 and VOYGR-6 plant configurations, allows prospective customers to reference the validated design in their Combined License Applications without repeating the full regulatory review. That shortcut is worth years and hundreds of millions of dollars to any utility willing to move first. The NRC certification process is, by design, a moat — one that took NuScale roughly fifteen years and more than $600 million in Fluor Corporation equity to cross.

The thesis for 2026–2030 is therefore simple to state and extraordinarily difficult to execute: NuScale must convert regulatory primacy into binding commercial contracts before its cash runway narrows, before rival technologies — domestic or European — close the certification gap, and before the capital markets lose patience with a story that has produced two NRC approvals and near-zero power-sale revenue. Three milestones will determine whether that conversion happens: a Final Investment Decision by RoPower Nuclear in Romania, a binding deployment agreement with the Tennessee Valley Authority, and a signed contract with at least one AI data-center operator seeking 24/7 carbon-free baseload.

## The Option-Value Arithmetic

The gap between NuScale's financial reality and its market valuation is not a bug in the pricing; it is the whole point.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Market capitalization (late May 2026) | ~$4.5 billion |
| FY2025 revenue | $31.5 million |
| Q1 2026 revenue | $0.6 million |
| Cash and short-term investments (Q1 2026 end) | ~$1.0 billion |
| Long-term debt | $0 |
| FY2025 net loss | ~$355.8 million |

[NuScale Q1 2026 earnings release](https://www.nuscalepower.com/press-releases/2026/nuscale-power-reports-first-quarter-2026-results); [NuScale FY2025 10-K via SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001822966/000182296626000018/smr-20251231.htm)

Full-year 2025 revenue of $31.5 million was itself episodic — driven primarily by the RoPower technology license fee and Romania engineering deliverables. When those contracts reached completion in late 2025, Q1 2026 revenue collapsed 95.5 percent year-over-year, confirming that NuScale's income stream is milestone-contingent rather than recurring. The company has never recorded a dollar of revenue from the sale of electricity or nuclear capacity. Every dollar it has ever earned has come from licensing fees, engineering services, or government cost-share reimbursements.

What sustains the $4.5 billion valuation is the $1.0 billion cash balance — product of a $750 million at-the-market equity raise in Q4 2025 — and the structural irreplaceability of the NRC approvals. No other U.S. SMR developer has either certification. That asymmetry, rather than any near-term earnings power, is what equity investors are pricing.

## The Three Commercial Linchpins

NuScale's path from option value to operating company runs through three discrete events, each of which is necessary but none of which, as of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, was contractually assured.

**Romania.** SN Nuclearelectrica's shareholders approved advancing the RoPower Doicești project following Fluor's completion of the Phase 2 FEED study in 2025, with a Final Investment Decision targeted for 2026 and first power from a six-module 462 MWe plant targeted around 2030. Romania represents NuScale's most engineering-mature engagement and its most credible near-term FID candidate — but a targeted decision is not a signed one, and European energy politics, financing structures, and construction-cost uncertainty remain live variables.

**TVA.** ENTRA1 Energy, NuScale's exclusive global commercialization partner, reached a non-binding collaborative agreement with the Tennessee Valley Authority in late 2025 for deployment of up to six gigawatts of NuScale capacity across TVA's seven-state service territory — a program management characterized as the largest nuclear deployment initiative in U.S. history. Non-binding is the operative word. No Combined License Application had been filed, no EPC contract signed, and no project financing secured as of the snapshot date.

**AI data centers.** Standard Power and unnamed hyperscale computing operators had engaged NuScale in advanced discussions as of Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 seeking grid-independent, always-on, carbon-free power for AI infrastructure. The sector's appetite for reliable baseload — which wind and solar cannot supply without storage at competitive cost — is the most compelling structural change in NuScale's addressable market since the UAMPS cancellation in 2023. A signed anchor contract with a named data-center customer would fundamentally reframe the commercialization narrative.

Each linchpin is plausible. None is probable on a specific timeline. That is what first-mover premiums cost.

chapters.title: Corporate History: From Oregon State University to NYSE — Three Near-Deaths and a Regulatory First
chapters.body:
## The Laboratory Idea

The origins of America's only certified small modular reactor trace not to a corporate boardroom but to a Department of Energy research contract issued in 2000 to Oregon State University. There, Dr. José N. Reyes Jr., a nuclear engineering professor, began testing a deceptively simple proposition: that the thermodynamic principles governing large pressurized water reactors could be reimagined at reduced scale, eliminating the active cooling pumps, diesel backup generators, and operator interventions that had made conventional nuclear so expensive to license and so catastrophic when they failed. Reyes and his colleague Dr. Paul G. Lorenzini incorporated NuScale Power in 2007 in Corvallis, Oregon, translating seven years of DOE-funded laboratory work into a commercial venture built around a single core insight — that a factory-built, passively safe, below-grade reactor module could be manufactured at industrial scale and assembled at customer sites in standardized increments, breaking the custom-civil-construction cost spiral that had plagued every American nuclear project of the prior generation.

The foundational intellectual property distinguished NuScale from predecessor research in two ways. First, the NuScale Power Module achieved natural circulation cooling without any primary coolant pumps — water circulated entirely through convective thermodynamics, so a loss of external power could not trigger a Fukushima-type cascade. Second, the module sat submerged in a below-grade pool, combining passive heat removal with seismic and security protection in a single architectural decision. These were not incremental refinements of existing designs but structural departures that the founders believed could finally make nuclear economics competitive with combined-cycle gas.

## The Fluor Rescue

The startup's early years demonstrated that regulatory ambition and venture capital are an uncomfortable pairing. NuScale had attracted a primary investor whose financial commitments underpinned the company's operating budget through its first years of design development. When federal investigators determined in 2011 that the investor had been operating a Ponzi scheme, NuScale's funding evaporated almost overnight. The company faced liquidation.

Fluor Corporation, the global engineering and construction giant, moved quickly. It acquired a majority interest in NuScale in 2011 for $3.5 million in acquisition consideration plus roughly $30 million in working capital infusion — a price that reflected the severity of the company's distress rather than any assessment of its technology's value. The transaction prevented the dissolution of a company that had spent more than a decade developing its core IP and was within reach of formal NRC engagement.

What followed was one of the more consequential long-term commitments in the history of private nuclear investment. Fluor did not merely rescue NuScale from insolvency; it funded the company through the entire pre-commercial period, ultimately deploying more than $600 million in cumulative capital through 2022. That investment covered NRC licensing fees, DOE cost-share matching obligations, engineering staff, test facility operations at OSU and at SIET S.p.A. in Italy, and the commercial development work that eventually produced the UAMPS partnership. In exchange, Fluor held approximately 55 percent of NuScale at the time of the 2022 SPAC listing — a concentration that would later become a structural overhang on the public stock but that had, in the preceding decade, provided the patient capital that no other counterparty was willing to commit.

## Fifteen Years to Certification

NuScale submitted its Design Certification Application to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in 2008, beginning what would become a fifteen-year regulatory odyssey. The NRC's review process for novel reactor designs has no established fast track; the agency must evaluate not just engineering documentation but the adequacy of the applicant's safety analysis methods, the completeness of its probabilistic risk assessments, and the physical testing record supporting passive-safety claims. The DOE provided critical cost-sharing support across two tranches — $226 million awarded in 2013 and $217 million in 2014 — that allowed NuScale to sustain engineering staffing through years of iterative NRC questions and design revisions.

The NRC issued its Final Safety Evaluation Report in August 2020, formally concluding that the NuScale design met all applicable safety standards. The Design Certification itself — the rule that allows any U.S. utility to reference the design in a Combined License Application without repeating the full safety review — was published in January 2023, making NuScale the first SMR developer in American history to achieve that status. The elapsed time from initial application to final rule: approximately fifteen years. No other U.S. SMR developer had cleared that bar as of the frozen snapshot date.

## UAMPS and the $9.3 Billion Reckoning

For much of the 2010s, NuScale's commercial strategy centered on a single flagship project: the Carbon Free Power Project, a proposed twelve-module, then six-module plant at Idaho National Laboratory developed in partnership with the Utah Associated Municipal Power Systems, a consortium of small Western utilities. UAMPS announced the project in 2014 and submitted formal design documents in 2017, giving NuScale its first named customer and its first public proof-of-concept for the modular deployment thesis.

The numbers, initially, were credible. In 2021 UAMPS projected an all-in cost for a six-module, 462 MWe plant at roughly $58 per megawatt-hour, competitive with new combined-cycle gas on a long-term levelized basis for utilities that valued carbon-free dispatch. Then costs accelerated. Inflation in engineered components, the absence of any comparable first-of-a-kind manufacturing baseline, and the carrying cost of a project that had been in development for nearly a decade pushed the January 2023 cost revision to $9.3 billion total — an increase that drove the projected per-MWh cost toward $90, against a Western renewable and gas market where comparable capacity could be procured at materially lower rates.

| Metric | 2021 Projection | Jan 2023 Revision |
|---|---|---|
| Plant capacity | 462 MWe (6 modules) | 462 MWe (6 modules) |
| Total project cost | ~$3.6 billion | $9.3 billion |
| Projected cost/MWh | ~$58 | ~$89–$90 |

UAMPS cancelled the Carbon Free Power Project in November 2023. NuScale announced a 28 percent workforce reduction — 154 employees — in the same period. The share price, which had already declined substantially from its post-SPAC highs, fell further on the news, completing a trajectory that had taken the stock from its 2022 listing levels to a fraction of that value within eighteen months.

## From SPAC to Public Markets

NuScale had entered public equity markets in May 2022 through a merger with Spring Valley Acquisition Corp, a special-purpose acquisition company sponsored by Pearl Energy Investments. The transaction generated approximately $380 million in gross proceeds and listed NuScale on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker SMR — a symbol that, for a period, carried the symbolic weight of an entire industry thesis about advanced nuclear's commercial future. The post-merger capital position was intended to fund NuScale through commercial contract execution and early project development.

The stock's trajectory proved instructive about market patience with pre-revenue deep-technology companies. NuScale listed into a period of elevated energy-sector enthusiasm, then descended through the UAMPS deterioration and cancellation into a prolonged trough. Fluor's subsequent systematic reduction of its stake — from approximately 55 percent at listing to roughly 7.8 percent by early 2026, sold through secondary placements to Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, and other institutional buyers — removed a structural overhang but simultaneously signaled that the company's founding patron had concluded its equity concentration in NuScale no longer warranted the exposure.

## Survival and the Rebound Thesis

The post-UAMPS period produced a company that was smaller, more focused, and paradoxically better positioned than the one that had entered the Idaho project. By Q4 2025, NuScale had executed a $750 million at-the-market equity raise — selling 39.3 million Class A shares and bringing year-end liquidity to approximately $1.3 billion with zero long-term debt. The capital base gave management a multi-year operating runway and removed the near-term financing risk that had suppressed the stock through 2024.

The NRC issued its Standard Design Approval for the uprated 77 MWe NPM design ahead of schedule in May 2025 — NuScale's second NRC design-level approval, confirming that the regulatory moat extended to the upgraded module configuration and applied to the VOYGR-4 and VOYGR-6 plant scales. Supply chain partner Doosan Enerbility in South Korea had begun forging long-lead components for twelve NuScale Power Modules, representing the most tangible manufacturing activity in the program's history.

ENTRA1 Energy, NuScale's exclusive global commercialization partner, reached a non-binding agreement with Tennessee Valley Authority in late 2025 to plan deployment of up to six gigawatts of NuScale SMR capacity across TVA's seven-state service territory — an arrangement management described as the largest nuclear deployment initiative in U.S. history. In Romania, Fluor completed its Phase 2 Front-End Engineering and Design study for the RoPower project at the Doicești power station, with shareholders of SN Nuclearelectrica approving advancement toward a Final Investment Decision targeted for 2026.

The company that emerged from fifteen years of regulatory work, a Ponzi-scheme rescue, and a $9.3 billion cost catastrophe carried a singular asset: the only active NRC design approvals for a small modular reactor in American history, a regulatory moat that no competitor had yet crossed, and a cash position sufficient to reach the binding commercial commitments that would determine whether the first-mover advantage proved durable.

chapters.title: Technology and Products: The NuScale Power Module, VOYGR Configurations, and the Passive Safety Proposition
chapters.body:
## The Machine at the Center of Everything

At the heart of NuScale Power's fifteen-year regulatory campaign sat a deceptively compact piece of engineering: the NuScale Power Module, a self-contained pressurized light water reactor measuring roughly 65 feet in height and 9 feet in diameter, capable of producing 77 megawatts of electricity or 250 megawatts of thermal energy from a single unit. The module operated at roughly 850 pounds per square inch of pressure, used low-enriched uranium in a standard 17×17 fuel assembly geometry identical to the fuel loaded into America's existing fleet of large pressurized water reactors, and required no active pumps, no diesel generators, and no operator intervention to reach a stable, cooled-down state following a trip or emergency. That last property — passive safety through physics rather than engineered redundancy — was the founding proposition, the source of NuScale's regulatory moat, and the argument that underpinned every commercial conversation the company conducted through the frozen snapshot date of May 2026.

The passive safety architecture worked on three interlocking principles. Primary coolant circulation relied entirely on natural convection: water heated by the reactor core rose into the once-through steam generator, transferred its heat to the secondary loop, cooled, and descended back to the core under gravity. No primary coolant pumps were required. In an emergency, the reactor's emergency core cooling system discharged water from a pressurized injection accumulator and then from gravity-fed tanks into the reactor vessel — no powered injection pumps, no AC bus required. Finally, the entire reactor and containment vessel assembly sat submerged in a below-grade pool of water that acted as an ultimate heat sink, providing days of passive decay heat removal without any active systems. The design's claimed seventy-two-hour no-action window — meaning no operator action, no AC power, and no additional water addition required for three full days following shutdown — was validated through integral system testing at Oregon State University's MASLWR test facility and at SIET S.p.A. in Italy, two physical facilities that gave NuScale's safety case an empirical foundation unusual for a pre-commercial reactor program.

## Two Certifications, One Uprate

The NRC's first approval of a NuScale design came in January 2023, when the agency issued its Design Certification for the original 50 MWe module configuration — the first and, as of the frozen snapshot date, only Design Certification ever granted to a small modular reactor by the United States Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The certification process had consumed roughly a decade of licensing work and generated the most voluminous safety review dossier the NRC had processed for any new reactor type in the modern era.

That 50 MWe certification, however, had already been superseded in engineering intent before the ink was dry. NuScale had been pursuing a power uprate to 77 MWe per module since at least 2020, driven by a straightforward economics argument: a larger thermal output from the same module envelope reduced the levelized capital cost per megawatt, improving the power price competitiveness of a VOYGR plant without requiring a redesigned civil structure or a new containment vessel. The uprate was achieved through changes to the steam generator design, operating pressure, and fuel enrichment level, while the passive safety architecture remained structurally unchanged. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued its Standard Design Approval for the 77 MWe configuration in May 2025 — ahead of schedule, management noted — making NuScale the only company in the world to hold two separate NRC approvals for an SMR design. The SDA, unlike the earlier Design Certification, applied specifically to the VOYGR-4 and VOYGR-6 plant configurations and allowed prospective customers to reference the approved design directly in their Combined License Applications without repeating the full multi-year design review, a material reduction in the regulatory burden and timeline for any customer moving toward construction.

## VOYGR: Scalable by Design

NuScale offered its technology in three plant configurations distinguished by module count:

| Configuration | Modules | Net Output (MWe) | Primary Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| VOYGR-4 | 4 | 308 | Utilities, industrial captive |
| VOYGR-6 | 6 | 462 | Mid-size utility, Romania RoPower |
| VOYGR-12 | 12 | 924 | Large utility, baseload replacement |

The modularity argument had two distinct commercial values. The first was right-sizing: a municipality or industrial customer unwilling to commit to a 924 MWe plant could contract for a VOYGR-4 at 308 MWe and expand to VOYGR-12 incrementally over time, adding modules to an already-operating plant without redesigning the reactor building or the balance of plant. Each module operated independently within the shared pool, so a four-module plant adding two additional modules did not require a full outage of existing units. The second value was risk distribution: the first-of-a-kind engineering costs and construction learning-curve inefficiencies that destroyed the UAMPS project at Idaho National Laboratory were theoretically amortizable across a larger installed base if multiple VOYGR plants could reference the same certified design, the same standard equipment packages, and the same installation methodology.

The RoPower project in Romania — a VOYGR-6 at the converted Doicești Power Station — and the Tennessee Valley Authority framework program were both structured to reference the 77 MWe Standard Design Approval, meaning the design work completed for NRC was directly portable to both engagements without country-specific redesign for the nuclear island.

## Factory-Made, Field-Assembled

The manufacturing and logistics model represented a deliberate departure from the bespoke, site-built approach that had inflated costs at every large nuclear project constructed in the United States and Europe since the 1980s. NuScale designed the NPM to be fabricated in a controlled factory environment — a heavy manufacturing facility of the kind operated by Doosan Enerbility in South Korea — and then transported to site by truck, rail, or barge. Module dimensions were constrained to fit within standard heavy-lift transport envelopes, enabling movement via existing road and rail infrastructure without the specialized over-dimensional transport problems that plagued large reactor pressure vessels.

At the site, each module was lowered into a standardized below-grade pool cavity. The below-grade installation reduced the structural requirements for the reactor building, improved resistance to seismic loading and external hazard events, and eliminated the above-grade reactor building profile that required expensive and complex structural engineering in conventional plant designs. Because the NPM used standard 17×17 LWR fuel geometry — the same form factor used in the operating Westinghouse AP1000 and conventional PWR fleets — the fuel fabrication supply chain required no new infrastructure. Framatome, the French nuclear engineering group, was engaged as a fuel supply partner with a specific mandate to support both U.S. and European delivery timelines, with an expanded partnership formalized in Q1 2026.

Doosan Enerbility's agreement to begin forging long-lead components for twelve NuScale Power Modules represented the most tangible manufacturing-readiness milestone in NuScale's history. Pressure vessel forgings, steam generator components, and other nuclear-grade heavy items require lead times measured in years; Doosan's commencement of this work before any commercial contract was fully closed signaled a level of supply chain commitment beyond what a pure licensing story would have generated.

## Beyond Electricity: Heat and Data Centers

NuScale completed an industrial process heat and cogeneration feasibility study in 2025 that validated the NPM's suitability for supplying combined steam and electricity to chemical plants, desalination facilities, and other heavy industrial processes that require both high-temperature heat and reliable power. The thermal output of 250 MWt per module — larger than the 77 MWe electrical figure — made the NPM potentially attractive for processes such as hydrogen production via high-temperature electrolysis, ammonia synthesis, and industrial steam supply, where the ability to extract thermal energy directly from the secondary loop without full conversion to electricity improved overall system efficiency. The study expanded NuScale's addressable market beyond regulated utilities into sectors where energy security and carbon reduction objectives were creating demand for alternatives to natural gas-fired process heat.

The AI data-center application emerged as perhaps the most commercially urgent product extension by late 2025. Hyperscale computing facilities operated by cloud and AI infrastructure companies were consuming power at a scale and with a reliability requirement that grid-connected intermittent renewables could not consistently satisfy. NuScale's management reported being in advanced dialogue with multiple data-center and AI infrastructure customers through Q1 2026, with Standard Power identified publicly as one operator seeking large-scale, grid-independent, carbon-free baseload. The VOYGR-4 at 308 MWe was positioned as an appropriately sized dedicated generation asset for a large campus-scale computing installation.

## Competitive Position

NuScale's technology occupied a distinct and intentional position in the SMR landscape.

| Developer | Design | Output/Unit | Coolant | NRC Status (as of May 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NuScale | NPM (VOYGR) | 77 MWe | Light water (PWR) | Design Cert (50 MWe, 2023) + SDA (77 MWe, 2025) |
| Rolls-Royce (UK) | UK SMR | ~470 MWe | Light water (PWR) | UK GDA in progress |
| TerraPower | Natrium | ~345 MWe (with storage) | Sodium-cooled fast | NRC pre-application |
| X-energy | Xe-100 | ~80 MWe | Helium (HTGR) | NRC pre-application |

Rolls-Royce's UK SMR operated at a fundamentally different scale — 470 MWe per unit — which changed its economic profile toward large utility projects and away from the distributed industrial or smaller-grid applications where NuScale's modularity carried most value. TerraPower's Natrium design used a sodium-cooled fast reactor architecture with integrated molten-salt thermal storage, a technically sophisticated system with different safety characteristics, different fuel requirements, and a regulatory pathway that had not yet produced any design approval from a major nuclear regulator. X-energy's Xe-100 was a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor using TRISO fuel pebbles and helium coolant — a fundamentally different safety and fuel cycle architecture with potential advantages in process heat temperature but a supply chain and regulatory track record far shorter than NuScale's.

NuScale's regulatory completeness was its most durable competitive advantage. An NRC Design Certification or Standard Design Approval was not a document that could be replicated in two or three years; the review process consumed the better part of a decade, involved millions of pages of safety analysis, and required resolution of every conceivable licensing basis question before approval was issued. No other SMR developer in the United States had reached that threshold by the frozen snapshot date, and the gap was measured not in months but in years of irreducible regulatory calendar.

chapters.title: Financial Deep Dive: Cash Burn, Milestone Accounting, and the Balance Sheet That Buys Time
chapters.body:
## The Number That Stops Readers Cold

Open NuScale Power's full-year 2025 income statement and a single line item arrests attention: general and administrative expense of $609.8 million, against $75.9 million the prior year. For a company that generated $31.5 million in revenue, the arithmetic implies an operating loss that dwarfs the entire enterprise. It implies, in the most literal reading, a business destroying roughly nineteen dollars for every dollar it earns. That reading is wrong, and the correction tells you almost everything important about how NuScale's finances actually work.

Of the $609.8 million G&A figure, $507.4 million represents the recognition of Milestone Contribution 1 under NuScale's [Partnership Milestone Agreement with ENTRA1 Energy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001822966/000182296626000018/smr-20251231.htm). This is a non-cash or milestone-contingent accounting item tied to ENTRA1's progress as NuScale's exclusive global commercialization partner — it does not represent $507.4 million in cash leaving the building. Strip the milestone contribution out and cash G&A expense runs at something far closer to the $75.9 million reported in FY2024, which is itself an elevated figure for a company with fewer than 600 employees. The GAAP loss for FY2025 was approximately $355.8 million; the cash operating burn was substantially lower. For investors trained on conventional income statements, the failure to parse this item is the most consequential analytical mistake one can make when approaching NuScale's financials.

The ENTRA1 partnership milestone structure works as follows: when ENTRA1 achieves defined commercialization milestones — licensing progress, customer agreements, deployment frameworks — NuScale recognizes a contribution expense that reflects the equity value or contingent consideration transferred to ENTRA1 under the original partnership construct. The Milestone Contribution 1 recognition in 2025 was tied to the progression of the TVA engagement and the broader commercialization framework ENTRA1 advanced during the year. It inflates GAAP expenses without generating a cash flow statement entry of equivalent magnitude. Period-to-period G&A comparisons are, accordingly, essentially meaningless without this adjustment.

## Revenue: A Three-Year Map of Episodic Income

NuScale's revenue history is best understood as a series of discrete engineering service and licensing events rather than a growing commercial franchise. The company has never recognized a dollar of revenue from power sales or capacity payments. What it earns comes from technology licensing fees, engineering consultancy contracts, and government cost-sharing reimbursements from the U.S. Department of Energy.

| Fiscal Period | Revenue | Primary Driver |
|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | *See 10-K* | DOE cost-share grants, early Romania engineering services |
| FY2024 | $37.0 million | RoPower Romania technology license fee, DOE cost-share reimbursements |
| FY2025 | $31.5 million | RoPower engineering services (Phase 2 FEED), residual DOE cost-share |
| Q1 2026 | $0.6 million | Minimal engineering service activity post-FEED completion |

The $37.0 million in FY2024 was driven primarily by recognition of the technology license fee associated with the RoPower agreement with SN Nuclearelectrica, Romania's state nuclear utility. That license fee represented a one-time contractual milestone; once booked, it did not recur. FY2025's $31.5 million reflected continued engineering deliverables under the Romania Phase 2 FEED program, but as that work completed in late 2025, the quarterly revenue run-rate collapsed. Q1 2026's $0.6 million against $13.4 million in Q1 2025 — a 95.5 percent year-over-year decline — confirmed the episodic, non-recurring character of the income stream. Cost of sales reached $20.0 million in FY2025 against $4.9 million the prior year, reflecting the expanded engineering headcount and subcontractor costs deployed on the Romania FEED deliverables. Gross margins are thin and variable; the company does not operate with the recurring revenue base that would support traditional margin analysis.

Investment income of $25.3 million in FY2025, up from $8.4 million in FY2024, is in this environment genuinely meaningful: a large, well-managed cash balance generates a return that partially offsets operating expenses. At a four-to-five percent short-duration yield on approximately $500-600 million in average cash and short-term investments held through most of 2025 (before the Q4 ATM proceeds arrived), the investment income line is not an accounting afterthought but a real offset to cash burn.

## Capital Structure: The Unusual Luxury of Debt-Free Survival

The most striking feature of NuScale's balance sheet — more striking, arguably, than any revenue or expense figure — is the absence of long-term debt. As of December 31, 2025, NuScale carried zero long-term debt against $1.3 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments. By the end of Q1 2026, following three months of operating expenditure, that figure had declined to approximately $1.0 billion.

At a cash operating burn — stripping non-cash items — of roughly $30 to $60 million per quarter (the range implied by the company's guidance language and pre-ATM cash consumption patterns), the current liquidity position represents between four and eight years of operating runway at the low end of that range, or two to four years at the high end. More realistically, maintaining the Romania FEED support, TVA planning engagement, Korea and Ghana technical relationships, and Poland KGHM engineering activity will require continued R&D and G&A expenditure in the $120 to $200 million cash range annually. On that basis, the $1.0 billion Q1 2026 liquidity represents approximately five to eight years of operating runway — an almost unprecedented duration for a pre-commercial nuclear developer.

This capital structure is the direct product of one decision: the $750 million ATM equity raise completed in Q4 2025.

## The ATM: Dilution Math and Strategic Logic

Between July and December 2025, NuScale sold 39.3 million Class A shares through an at-the-market equity program, generating $750 million in gross proceeds. With 39.3 million shares sold and $750 million raised, the implied average sale price was approximately $19.08 per share — a level well above the stock's position in late May 2026 (around $12.29) but well below the 52-week high of $57.42. This timing reflects both NuScale's opportunism in capturing elevated prices during a period of SMR enthusiasm and the necessity of locking in runway before commercialization timelines clarified.

The dilution impact is real. Existing shareholders at the time of the ATM absorbed approximately 39.3 million new shares against a then-outstanding share count that, combined with warrants and founder shares from the 2022 SPAC, puts the fully diluted count in the range of several hundred million shares. The percentage dilution, while meaningful, was traded against a liquidity position that effectively eliminates near-term financing risk — the existential threat for any pre-commercial energy technology company. Management's implicit argument: accept dilution now and preserve the option value; refuse dilution and risk being forced to the market in a distressed position.

## Fluor's Long Exit and What It Cost

Fluor Corporation's relationship with NuScale is the founding financial story of the company. When NuScale's original primary investor was investigated for operating a Ponzi scheme in 2011, threatening to strand the research program at Oregon State University, Fluor stepped in — acquiring a majority interest for $3.5 million plus approximately $30 million in working capital. Over the subsequent decade, Fluor's cumulative investment exceeded $600 million, making it simultaneously the company's savior and its most consequential creditor-turned-shareholder.

At the May 2022 SPAC merger close, Fluor held approximately 55 percent of NuScale. By April 2026, [that position had been reduced to roughly 7.8 percent](https://www.nuscalepower.com/investors/annual-reports) through a systematic series of secondary block sales, with Goldman Sachs and Bank of America serving as the principal institutional buyers in major transactions. The divestiture has been orderly rather than distressed — Fluor executed at market prices over multiple transactions rather than dumping a concentrated position — but it has produced two identifiable effects.

First, it removed a strategic anchor shareholder. Fluor's 55 percent stake, while creating its own governance complexities, provided an implicit floor of institutional credibility. Its reduction to single-digit ownership signals that Fluor has concluded its strategic rationale for NuScale concentration has passed, even if it retains a residual position.

Second, the mathematics of Fluor's recovery relative to its investment are uncomfortable. At the 52-week high of $57.42, the shares Fluor has sold and retained carried a combined market value that could have represented a substantial recovery against its $600 million-plus investment. At $12.29 — the late May 2026 price — the calculus is considerably less favorable. The shares Fluor sold in block trades to Goldman and Bank of America were transacted at prices that likely varied considerably across the divestiture timeline; without precise per-block pricing the exact recovery is unclear, but it is almost certain that the bulk of Fluor's $600 million investment has not been recouped at realized sale prices.

## The Forward Burn: What the Runway Actually Has to Cover

The $1.0 billion in Q1 2026 liquidity must fund a specific set of obligations through the critical 2026-2027 commercialization window:

The Romania FEED continuation and pre-FID engineering support requires sustained NuScale technical resources. The TVA planning engagement — non-binding but diplomatically essential — requires licensing and regulatory support staff capable of responding to TVA's internal engineering queries and Combined License Application groundwork. The Doosan Enerbility manufacturing preparedness program, while funded primarily by Doosan, requires NuScale engineering interfaces for the twelve-module long-lead component fabrication underway in South Korea. Korea, Ghana, and Poland relationships each require dedicated technical and business development resources. The Framatome fuel partnership expansion announced in Q1 2026 adds fuel supply chain engineering costs.

Against this, NuScale earns essentially nothing in recurring revenue until a customer reaches Final Investment Decision with committed financing. The company's own commentary acknowledges that quarterly cash consumption in the $30 to $60 million range is the operating reality. At the midpoint of $45 million per quarter, the $1.0 billion Q1 2026 cash position represents approximately five and a half years of runway — through roughly late 2031. At the high end of $60 million per quarter, the runway compresses to approximately four years, reaching into mid-2030.

The strategic implication is that NuScale does not need to execute a commercial contract in 2026 or 2027 to avoid a financing crisis. But the equity market's patience has limits that balance sheet math does not capture. With the share price down from $57.42 to $12.29 in twelve months, and Q1 2026 revenue at $0.6 million, investors are already reassessing whether the commercialization timeline implied by management's pipeline commentary can be reconciled with the lumpy, engineering-fee revenue profile that is NuScale's near-term financial reality. The balance sheet buys time. Whether management uses that time to convert Romania and TVA from engineering engagements into binding contracts will determine whether the ATM's dilution was a masterstroke of financial runway management or the beginning of a longer, more painful dilution cycle.

chapters.title: Earnings Story: Quarterly Cadence, Management Commentary, and the Revenue Cliff of Q1 2026
chapters.body:
## A Calendar of Consequences

For most publicly traded companies, the quarterly earnings cycle functions as a periodic financial report card. For NuScale Power Corporation, it functions as something closer to a series of investor confidence hearings — procedural exercises in narrative maintenance at a moment when the company's income statement offers almost nothing in the way of conventional performance signals. Understanding NuScale's earnings arc from early 2025 through the first quarter of 2026 requires accepting a foundational premise: until the company executes a binding commercial contract with committed financing, quarterly revenue figures are best read as proxies for contract timing, not business health.

With that framing in place, the story of fiscal year 2025 becomes considerably more legible.

## The FY2025 Arc: Strong Opening, Fading Middle, Transformative Close

NuScale entered 2025 on the back of its second NRC design certification — a regulatory milestone that transformed the company's commercial conversation from theoretical to near-executable — and with its Romania FEED (Front-End Engineering and Design) program generating a meaningful stream of technology licensing and engineering services fees. The first quarter of 2025 delivered [revenue of $13.4 million](https://www.nuscalepower.com/investors/quarterly-results), the strongest single-quarter result the company would post all year, driven by drawdowns under the RoPower technology license agreement and early FEED deliverables. Against a full-year 2024 comparable of $37.0 million, the pace suggested the company might sustain or exceed that benchmark.

It did not. As the Romania FEED program moved through its defined engineering phases and milestone payments were recognized, the revenue cadence grew lumpier through the middle quarters of the year. The program's structure — discrete deliverables triggering license and services payments rather than a steady contractual stream — meant that revenue recognition was always going to cluster at phase completions. The second and third quarters combined to fill out the annual tally, but with diminishing quarter-on-quarter contributions as the FEED program approached its late-2025 conclusion.

Full-year 2025 revenue came in at [$31.5 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001822966/000182296626000018/smr-20251231.htm), a decline from the $37.0 million recorded in fiscal 2024. Cost of sales jumped sharply to $20.0 million from $4.9 million in the prior year, reflecting the expanded engineering workforce and deliverable scope required to complete the Romania FEED. The gross contribution from operations narrowed materially, though this was largely expected given the front-loaded nature of the program.

The more arresting figure in the fiscal 2025 income statement was the G&A expense line: $609.8 million, versus $75.9 million in 2024. This number is nearly useless as an operating metric. The overwhelming majority of the increase — $507.4 million — reflects the recognition of Milestone Contribution 1 under the Partnership Milestone Agreement with ENTRA1 Energy, a non-cash accounting entry tied to the announcement of the TVA-adjacent 6-gigawatt SMR program. Strip that item, and cash G&A expenses were far lower. The GAAP net loss of approximately $355.8 million must be read with the same asterisk.

What the fourth quarter actually delivered, beyond accounting complexity, was a financial transformation of the balance sheet. A $750 million at-the-market equity offering — selling 39.3 million Class A shares — closed in Q4 2025 and vaulted the company's cash, equivalents, and short-term investments to [$1.3 billion at year-end](https://www.nuscalepower.com/press-releases/2026/nuscale-power-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results), against zero long-term debt. The company entered 2026 with the most durable liquidity position in its public history and, for the first time, a runway measured in years rather than quarters.

## Hopkins at Year-End: Framing the Inflection

At the Q4 2025 earnings call in late February 2026, chief executive John Hopkins used the occasion to characterize the prior year as a foundational turning point. He pointed to the TVA announcement — the framework agreement with ENTRA1 Energy for a potential 6-gigawatt SMR deployment program in the eastern United States — and to the completion of the Romania FEED as twin validation events that together defined what he described as a breakthrough year for the company's commercial positioning. The 6-gigawatt framing was deliberate: it signalled not a single plant order but a programme-scale commitment of the kind that would justify the capital investment required to stand up a domestic SMR supply chain. Romania, meanwhile, had moved from technology selection through engineering design to a point where a Final Investment Decision was at least theoretically within reach in 2026.

The year-end commentary also emphasized the structural cleanliness of the balance sheet as an enabler of patient execution — a management team communicating that it could afford to wait for the right commercial terms rather than accept inadequate ones under funding pressure.

## The Q1 2026 Revenue Cliff

Nothing in the management narrative prepared analysts for the arithmetic of the first quarter of 2026. Revenue collapsed to [$0.6 million](https://www.nuscalepower.com/press-releases/2026/nuscale-power-reports-first-quarter-2026-results), down 95.5 percent from the $13.4 million posted in Q1 2025. The reported EPS came in at -$0.14, a penny below the consensus estimate of -$0.13. Against a Wall Street consensus revenue forecast of approximately $4.99 million, the actual result represented a miss of roughly 88 percent.

| Quarter | Revenue | YoY Change | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 2025 | $13.4 million | — | Romania FEED, RoPower license fees |
| FY2025 Full Year | $31.5 million | -14.9% vs FY2024 | Romania FEED completion, ENTRA1 milestone (non-cash) |
| Q1 2026 | $0.6 million | -95.5% YoY | Post-FEED contract gap |

The proximate explanation was mechanical: the Romania FEED program had concluded its major engineering deliverables in late 2025, and no replacement contract of equivalent scope had commenced billing. NuScale's revenue model has never included recurring contracted revenues; every dollar recognized to date has flowed from a specific agreement for specific work. When that work ends and its successor has not yet been formally initiated, the income statement goes quiet.

Management's framing of the Q1 2026 result was therefore almost entirely forward-looking. The substantive disclosures were not financial but commercial: confirmation that RoPower's Romanian shareholders had approved the project's progression toward FID — a governance hurdle that had been a prerequisite for accessing certain European and multilateral financing facilities — and an update on the Framatome fuel supply partnership, which expanded in scope to encompass additional fuel fabrication commitments aligned with NuScale's VOYGR design specifications. Both items were positioned as pipeline-advancing events in a quarter that offered little else for investors to price.

## Analyst Reaction and the Consensus Problem

The 88 percent miss against consensus revenue raised an immediate interpretive question: did analysts actually expect $4.99 million, or had the consensus figure failed to incorporate publicly available information about the FEED program's completion timeline? Available commentary in the weeks following the result suggested the latter. Several sell-side desks had evidently rolled forward prior-quarter revenue run rates without fully discounting for the known contract gap, producing a consensus that reflected modelling inertia rather than genuine commercial expectation. The reaction to the print was accordingly muted relative to the size of the numerical miss — investors who had tracked the FEED program's completion milestones were not surprised by a near-zero quarter.

More substantive was the reaction to the share price, which had already retreated sharply from its 52-week high of $57.42 to trade near $12.29 by late May 2026 — a correction of approximately 79 percent from peak that reflected, more broadly, a reassessment of commercialization timelines across the SMR sector rather than specific doubts about NuScale's technology or regulatory position.

## Earnings as Narrative, Not Scorecard

The deeper lesson of NuScale's quarterly earnings cycle is structural. A company that has never sold a kilowatt-hour of electricity, that recognizes revenue only when an engineering milestone is achieved or a license fee is contractually triggered, and that carries no long-term debt against $1.0 billion in Q1 2026 liquidity is not a company whose income statement can be read through a conventional lens. Its quarterly calls are better understood as regulated investor communications in which the financial figures serve primarily as compliance disclosure, while the real content — commercial pipeline updates, regulatory progress markers, partnership expansions — is delivered in the prepared remarks and Q&A.

By that metric, Q1 2026 was not a bad quarter. Romania's shareholder approval was a genuine milestone. The Framatome fuel partnership expansion confirmed that the industrial supply chain was treating NuScale's commercialization as a probability rather than a possibility. The $1.0 billion liquidity position ensured that the narrative could continue undisturbed. What Q1 2026 was, above all, was a reminder that for NuScale, earnings calls measure the velocity of a story — and in early 2026, that story was still being written.

chapters.title: Leadership: Hopkins's Thirteen-Year Tenure, the Post-Crisis CFO, and a Board Rebuilt for Credibility
chapters.body:
## The Professional Manager and the Inventor's Chair

When John L. Hopkins assumed the presidency of NuScale Power in December 2012, replacing co-founder Paul Lorenzini, the move was unusual enough to merit examination. Lorenzini had been the company's animating force since its incorporation in 2007 — a former utility executive who had assembled the founding team around Oregon State University research and staked NuScale's early identity on his own commercial judgment. Replacing a founder at the helm of a deep-technology startup in the licensing phase, before a single dollar of commercial revenue had been recognized, is typically the kind of governance intervention that happens after failure. In NuScale's case it was a precautionary move by a controlling shareholder that had already written a rescue check.

Fluor Corporation had stepped in the prior year after NuScale's original primary investor was found to have been running a Ponzi scheme, committing what would ultimately become more than $600 million in equity and engineering labor. The acquisition of a majority interest gave Fluor the standing to shape the management structure, and what Fluor wanted — given the scale of capital it was deploying and the decade-plus commercialization timeline ahead — was not an inventor-evangelist running the enterprise. It wanted a professional manager: someone fluent in nuclear licensing bureaucracy, comfortable with government contracting, capable of managing a multi-decade capital program without founder-syndrome stubbornness. Hopkins, whose prior career had included executive roles at General Atomics and nuclear defense program management, fit that profile. His appointment signaled that NuScale was being run as an industrial program, not a startup.

Thirteen years later, Hopkins remains in place — a tenure that spans the company's entire public existence and virtually every material development in its commercial history. That longevity is itself a governance data point, reflecting both institutional continuity and the absence of a credible succession structure.

## Three Tests of a Thirteen-Year CEO

The first test was capital. The May 2022 SPAC merger with Spring Valley Acquisition Corp brought NuScale to the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker SMR, raising approximately $380 million in gross proceeds and valuing the company at roughly $1.9 billion. For Hopkins, the listing represented a transformation in the company's external accountability — from a closely held Fluor subsidiary operating under government cost-share agreements to a public company with quarterly reporting obligations and a share price as a daily referendum on management credibility. The mechanics of the listing, through a SPAC rather than a traditional IPO, drew scrutiny it always does for pre-revenue companies in capital-intensive sectors. Hopkins's task was to make the case that NuScale's regulatory franchise — its pending NRC design certification — constituted real, durable value. The stock initially reflected that argument, peaking above $15 in mid-2022 before the second test arrived.

The November 2023 UAMPS cancellation was the nearest thing to an existential crisis the company had survived on Hopkins's watch. The Carbon Free Power Project at Idaho National Laboratory, which had represented NuScale's flagship first-of-a-kind deployment, collapsed when the projected all-in cost for 462 MWe rose to $9.3 billion — from $3.6 billion for a larger 720 MWe configuration as recently as 2020 — and the estimated levelized cost of electricity approached $90 per megawatt-hour at a moment when natural gas and utility-scale solar were pricing power well below that threshold. Twelve of the fourteen UAMPS member utilities had withdrawn. The project's failure was a direct public challenge to the economic logic of the NuScale model.

Hopkins responded with a restructuring that cut 154 positions, 28 percent of the workforce, and a communications pivot that framed the UAMPS cancellation not as a product failure but as a demand-side mismatch — the wrong customer configuration for a cost structure that required a larger installed base to amortize. Whether that framing persuades depends on what comes next. The stock fell sharply in the weeks following the cancellation, and the company entered 2024 with its commercial pipeline consisting primarily of non-binding agreements and engineering studies.

The third test — the one Hopkins was building toward through 2025 — was commercial recovery. The combination of the ENTRA1/TVA 6-gigawatt framework agreement, the Phase 2 FEED completion in Romania, and the $750 million ATM raise in Q4 2025 gave management the narrative architecture of a turnaround: a credible U.S. deployment vehicle, an advanced European project approaching final investment decision, and a balance sheet ($1.3 billion in cash and investments, zero long-term debt) sufficient to reach binding commitment without distress financing. Hopkins's total compensation for FY2024 was reported at approximately $3.43 million, with roughly 82 percent weighted toward equity and performance-based awards — a structure that aligns his financial interest tightly with the commercialization milestones the company must hit to justify its valuation.

## Hamady and the Capital Markets Pivot

The appointment of Ramsey Hamady as Chief Financial Officer in August 2023 — arriving just as the UAMPS crisis was approaching its denouement — marked a deliberate reset in the financial leadership profile. Hamady's background ran through Equify Financial and Western Magnesium Corporation, organizations operating at a scale and complexity well below NuScale's current ambitions. What he brought was not sector-specific nuclear finance expertise but something the post-UAMPS company arguably needed more urgently: fluency with public company capital markets mechanics, SEC reporting, and the investor relations credibility required to execute a large-scale equity program.

That judgment was validated by the $750 million ATM execution in Q4 2025. At-the-market programs at this scale — 39.3 million Class A shares placed across institutional buyers — require careful coordination of disclosure timing, share price management, and investor positioning. Hamady's role in structuring and executing that raise was the primary proof point of his tenure. His prior experience at smaller companies does raise a legitimate question about whether his background adequately prepared him for the forward demands of the role: structuring project finance for multi-billion-dollar nuclear plants, negotiating the financial terms of the Romania FID, and managing the capital requirements of a TVA combined license application process. Those tasks will test a CFO profile built on equity market execution rather than structured project finance.

## Boeckmann, Board Independence, and the Role Separation Signal

The installation of Alan Boeckmann as Non-Executive Chairman effective January 15, 2025, was a governance improvement that institutional proxy advisors had been pushing the company toward for several years. Separating the board chair and CEO roles eliminates a structural concentration of authority that allows a long-tenured CEO to effectively control both the management function and the oversight function. Boeckmann is a credible appointment for the role: his career at Fluor — where he served as chairman and CEO — gives him direct familiarity with large-scale nuclear and energy infrastructure project execution, and his network within the engineering procurement and construction industry is directly relevant to NuScale's EPC contracting requirements. Whether the role separation reflects investor pressure or proactive governance self-improvement is ultimately a question about sequencing: the move came approximately fifteen months after the UAMPS crisis, at a moment when institutional investor trust was being rebuilt. The timing suggests responsiveness to external expectations rather than purely internal governance evolution.

## The Board Matrix

The nine-member board covers the principal qualification domains a pre-commercial nuclear company in the commercialization phase requires, with varying degrees of strategic depth behind each appointment.

| Director | Primary Qualification | Strategic Relationship |
|---|---|---|
| Alan Boeckmann | EPC/industrial infrastructure (Fluor CEO) | NRC licensing and project execution |
| Bum-Jin Chung | Korean industrial / nuclear supply chain | Doosan Enerbility and Korean supply chain |
| Shinji Fujino | Japanese industrial / nuclear sector | Japanese utility and regulatory relationships |
| Stuart Harshaw | Nuclear operations (utility executive) | Operational readiness and utility customer dialogue |
| John L. Hopkins | CEO / nuclear licensing | Management continuity |
| Dale Klein | Former NRC Chairman (2006–2009) | Regulatory relationships and licensing credibility |
| Kent Kresa | Defense / aerospace (Northrop Grumman) | Government contracting and defense-adjacent markets |
| Diana Walters | Finance / capital markets | Institutional investor credibility |
| Kimberly Warnica | Legal / corporate governance | Compliance and board process |

Bum-Jin Chung and Shinji Fujino's board seats warrant specific scrutiny. The representation of Korean and Japanese industrial interests at board level almost certainly reflects the Doosan Enerbility supply chain partnership — Doosan has begun forging long-lead components for twelve NuScale Power Modules — and the broader strategic importance of Asian nuclear manufacturing capacity to NuScale's cost-reduction thesis. Whether these seats represent governance of commercial relationships or primarily symbolic alignment with supply chain partners is not entirely clear from public disclosures, but their presence provides ongoing communication channels with the industrial infrastructure NuScale needs to deliver manufactured modules at projected costs.

Dale Klein's background as NRC Chairman from 2006 to 2009 is routinely cited in governance materials as a regulatory credential. The practical benefit deserves measured assessment. Klein's tenure at the NRC predates the NPM design review by roughly a decade; the NRC staff who evaluated NuScale's design certification and Standard Design Approval were operating under subsequent leadership and evolved review methodologies. Board-level NRC alumni presence does not accelerate or influence regulatory staff technical reviews. Klein's value to the board is more accurately characterized as institutional familiarity with the agency's culture, vocabulary, and process architecture — useful background for a board governing a company whose entire value proposition depends on regulatory outcomes, but not a regulatory shortcut.

## Fluor's Exit and the Governance It Left Behind

Fluor's reduction of its NuScale ownership from approximately 55 percent at the 2022 SPAC merger to roughly 7.8 percent by early 2026 represents one of the most consequential governance transitions in the company's history. As the controlling shareholder, Fluor had effectively backstopped NuScale's board composition, capital allocation decisions, and strategic direction for more than a decade. Its exit — executed through secondary share sales to Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, and other institutional buyers — removed that structural backstop. Fluor has characterized its divestiture publicly as a capital allocation decision reflecting its own balance sheet priorities, but the scale and pace of the share sales, spread across 2025 and into early 2026, also reflect a shareholder choosing to monetize a position rather than deepen it during the pivotal commercialization window. After more than $600 million in cumulative investment, Fluor's return at prevailing share prices represents a fraction of its capital commitment.

The governance implication is that NuScale now operates with a more dispersed institutional shareholder base and no single anchor investor with the incentive to intervene in a crisis the way Fluor did in 2011. Board representation tracked Fluor's ownership concentration: as the stake fell, Fluor's effective board influence diminished correspondingly, leaving a board that is nominally independent but was assembled during a period of Fluor oversight.

## The ENTRA1 Governance Gap

The governance question the proxy filings do not resolve is the absence of any ENTRA1 representation on the board. ENTRA1 Energy holds exclusive global commercialization rights to NuScale's technology, and the company recognized $507.4 million as Milestone Contribution 1 under its Partnership Milestone Agreement with ENTRA1 in FY2025 — making ENTRA1 effectively NuScale's largest single economic counterparty and the primary driver of the elevated G&A expense line ($609.8 million in FY2025 versus $75.9 million in FY2024). The Habboush Group is identified as a principal behind ENTRA1, but no member of the Habboush Group holds a disclosed board seat, committee role, or named advisory position in NuScale's proxy filings. For a relationship of this commercial centrality — one whose execution will determine whether the TVA program converts from framework agreement to binding contract — the absence of ENTRA1 representation in the governance structure is a disclosure gap that institutional investors should press management to explain. Whether this reflects deliberate structural separation, regulatory sensitivity around nuclear ownership disclosure requirements, or the informality of a relationship still being formalized is not answerable from public filings alone.

chapters.title: Customers and Markets: TVA's 6-Gigawatt Vision, Romania's Coal Conversion, and the AI Baseload Opportunity
chapters.body:
## The Architecture of a Pipeline

NuScale Power has never sold a kilowatt-hour. As of the frozen snapshot date in May 2026, the company's entire commercial edifice rests on a tiered portfolio of customer relationships ranging from binding engineering contracts worth tens of millions of dollars to aspirational framework agreements covering gigawatts of capacity that exist, for now, only in slide decks and press releases. Understanding NuScale's market position requires distinguishing clearly between these tiers — and identifying which, if any, is close enough to a Final Investment Decision to justify the company's roughly $4.5 billion market capitalization.

## Tennessee Valley Authority and the ENTRA1 Structure

The largest and most widely cited customer commitment is the non-binding collaborative agreement between ENTRA1 Energy and Tennessee Valley Authority, announced in the fourth quarter of 2025, covering deployment of up to six gigawatts of NuScale SMR capacity across TVA's seven-state service territory encompassing Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, Kentucky, Georgia, North Carolina, and Virginia. Management called it the largest nuclear deployment initiative in U.S. history — a characterization that is technically accurate and simultaneously almost meaningless, because no binding capital commitment existed as of the frozen snapshot date.

The ENTRA1 structure deserves scrutiny. NuScale itself is not TVA's counterparty. ENTRA1 Energy, which holds exclusive global commercialization rights to NuScale technology under a 2022 alliance with the Habboush Group, functions as the intermediary — deploying capital, holding project agreements, and taking on commercial risk that NuScale's balance sheet does not absorb directly. The arrangement insulates NuScale from the UAMPS-style overrun dynamic in which NuScale sat exposed as a technology licensor while cost estimates ballooned and utility off-takers defected. But it also means that the six-gigawatt headline number is doubly contingent: it requires both ENTRA1 to execute as a project developer and TVA to convert its collaborative engagement into site-specific Combined License Applications filed with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

TVA is an unusual counterparty for an SMR program. As a federally chartered corporation operating the largest public power system in the United States, it is not subject to state public utility commission rate-making in the conventional sense, which eliminates one layer of regulatory approval needed at investor-owned utilities. TVA has existing nuclear infrastructure — Browns Ferry and Watts Bar — and institutional nuclear competency. What it lacks, as of the frozen snapshot, is a completed NRC site permit application for a NuScale deployment, a secured engineering-procurement-construction contract with a fixed-price structure, and a committed financing package for even the first plant. Each of those milestones is a multi-year process. The six-gigawatt figure assumes roughly eight to twelve VOYGR-6 plants built sequentially over a decade or more. The first binding capital commitment, if it comes, will be for a single demonstration plant of 462 MWe — and even that has not been formally proposed.

## Romania: Coal to Carbon-Free

The more advanced customer engagement, by every measurable engineering metric, is [RoPower Nuclear](https://www.nuscalepower.com), the joint venture between NuScale and SN Nuclearelectrica, Romania's state nuclear utility and operator of the Cernavodă CANDU reactors. The RoPower project centers on a six-module VOYGR-6 plant at the Doicești Power Station in Dâmbovița County, a former coal generation site that the Romanian government designated for clean energy conversion as part of its decarbonization commitments.

The project's timeline is more concrete than TVA's. Fluor completed its Phase 2 Front-End Engineering and Design study for the Doicești plant during 2025, with engineering work conducted partly from the Romanian site. SN Nuclearelectrica's shareholders subsequently approved advancing to the next project phase, a formal milestone that establishes board-level Romanian commitment. The total estimated project cost ranges from $6 billion to $7 billion for the full six-module configuration. The Final Investment Decision is targeted for 2026, with commercial operations projected for approximately 2030.

The financing picture involves multiple public-sector actors. The U.S. Export-Import Bank, U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, and Export Credit Agencies from allied nations have all been cited as prospective funding sources for the Romanian project, reflecting the geopolitical dimension of deploying American nuclear technology in a NATO member state on the European Union's eastern flank. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development has conducted due diligence on the project. [NuScale's technology license revenue in FY2025 was principally derived from the RoPower engagement](https://www.nuscalepower.com/investors/annual-reports), underscoring that Romania is already the company's primary commercial revenue source even before FID.

NuScale and Framatome expanded their fuel supply partnership in Q1 2026 to support accelerated delivery timelines for both U.S. and European markets, with the RoPower schedule a primary driver. A secured domestic fuel supply chain has been a recurring concern for European SMR programs; the Framatome expansion directly addresses that constraint.

## Industrial and International Market Development

Beyond TVA and Romania, NuScale maintains customer relationships at earlier stages of development that serve primarily as market validation rather than near-term revenue.

KGHM Polska Miedź, the Polish state copper and silver mining conglomerate, signed a contract in 2022 for a NuScale SMR deployment in Poland, targeting a construction start date of 2029. KGHM's interest reflects a genuine industrial logic: copper smelting and refining operations are among the most electricity-intensive processes in heavy industry, and Poland's grid is still heavily coal-dependent, creating both carbon exposure and energy security risk for a company seeking European market access. The 2029 construction-start target had not been formally revised in subsequent NuScale disclosures as of the frozen snapshot date, though the Polish regulatory pathway remains in early stages and the schedule carries execution risk.

Ghana represents the company's market development investment in Sub-Saharan Africa. In August 2024, NuScale signed an agreement with Ghanaian nuclear authorities for a twelve-module plant, and in January 2025 opened a NuScale SMR simulator training center in the country. The training center is a meaningful signal of sustained commitment — simulator infrastructure typically precedes licensing and operations by a decade or more — but the Ghana program is unlikely to produce binding investment decisions within the dossier period. Its value lies in establishing NuScale as a credible long-term partner for emerging nuclear markets rather than in near-term capital formation.

## The AI Baseload Opportunity

The most economically novel element of NuScale's current commercial positioning is its engagement with AI data-center operators. The argument is structurally compelling: hyperscale computing campuses running large language model training and inference require power that is always available, uninterrupted, and increasingly under pressure from corporate Scope 2 emissions commitments. Wind and solar cannot meet the always-on requirement without large-scale battery storage, and the economics of battery storage at gigawatt-scale remain challenging. A NuScale VOYGR-6 plant at 462 MWe provides continuous, weather-independent, carbon-free baseload power — precisely what a 500-megawatt data center campus needs.

Standard Power, a U.S. data center developer, emerged as a publicly identified interested party in NuScale's SMR program. Beyond Standard Power, NuScale disclosed in its Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 earnings calls that it was in advanced dialogue with multiple unnamed data-center and AI infrastructure customers seeking grid-independent baseload power. The company has not disclosed contract terms, pricing structures, or timelines for any of these engagements, and none had progressed to a signed agreement as of the frozen snapshot date.

The economics require scrutiny. NuScale's VOYGR-6 plant at Doicești is projected to cost $6-7 billion for 462 MWe — a capital cost of roughly $13,000 to $15,000 per installed kilowatt. At a financing cost of seven percent and a forty-year operating life, that capital alone implies a levelized cost of electricity well above $80 per megawatt-hour before fuel and operations. Hyperscale operators currently pay $50-70/MWh for large long-term power purchase agreements with solar and wind. The AI baseload premium — the price customers will pay for guaranteed uptime and zero-carbon attributes — is real but has not yet been benchmarked against NuScale's cost structure in disclosed commercial terms.

## Which Customer Will Close First?

Assessed against engineering progress, financing structure, and regulatory pathway, Romania is the most likely candidate to produce the first binding commercial contract before 2027. The FEED engineering is complete, the shareholder approval milestone has passed, a defined FID target exists, and European public-sector financing architecture is available. TVA's six-gigawatt program, while larger in ultimate scale, lacks site-specific licensing progress and has no committed EPC structure. KGHM Poland's 2029 construction-start target requires a regulatory pathway that has not yet cleared equivalent milestones. The AI data-center engagements remain pre-contract.

Romania's risk is not engineering — it is political and financing sequencing. Export credit agencies from multiple governments must align, Romanian energy pricing must support the project's debt service, and the Nuclearelectrica board must navigate domestic politics around a $6-7 billion commitment. If any of those threads fray, NuScale's path to its first closed commercial contract extends beyond the horizon of the current dossier period. The company's $1.3 billion cash balance buys time, but the clock on investor patience, visible in the share price's decline from $57.42 to the mid-teens, is already running.

chapters.title: Competitive Position: NRC Moat Versus Global SMR Field and the Cost-Per-MWh Battleground
chapters.body:
## Two Arenas, One Balance Sheet

NuScale Power does not face a single competitive threat — it faces two simultaneously, and conflating them produces a distorted picture of the company's strategic position. The first arena is the race among SMR developers for technology credibility, customer contracts, and regulatory standing. The second is the deeper contest against every other form of reliable baseload power — combined-cycle gas, large conventional nuclear, and offshore wind paired with storage — on the only metric that ultimately determines whether a plant gets built: cost per megawatt-hour delivered to the grid. NuScale leads decisively in the first arena. It remains challenged in the second. The company's survival and ultimate commercial success depend on whether the structural changes introduced by the TVA framework and the RoPower program can close that gap before a well-capitalized competitor catches up on regulatory status.

## The U.S. SMR Regulatory Scoreboard

The domestic SMR competitive landscape is frequently described as crowded. In regulatory reality, it is not. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission's design certification and standard design approval processes are multi-year, hundred-million-dollar undertakings that impose brutal selection pressure. As of the frozen snapshot in May 2026, NuScale was the only U.S. company to have completed that process — twice.

Its first design certification, for the original 50-megawatt-electric NuScale Power Module, was issued in January 2023, making it the first SMR design certified by the NRC in the agency's history. The second approval — a Standard Design Approval for the uprated 77 MWe NPM covering VOYGR-4 and VOYGR-6 plant configurations — arrived ahead of schedule in May 2025. That SDA allows customers to reference the approved design in Combined License Applications without repeating the full design review, a procedural advantage of enormous commercial value.

The four principal U.S. challengers occupy substantially earlier regulatory positions.

| Developer | Reactor Type | Lead Project | NRC Status (as of May 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|
| TerraPower | Natrium (sodium-cooled fast) | Kemmerer, Wyoming | Construction permit application filed; no design certification |
| X-energy | Xe-100 (high-temperature gas) | ARDP award recipient | Pre-application engagement; no design certification |
| Kairos Power | KP-FHR (fluoride salt-cooled) | Hermes demonstration, Tennessee | Construction permit received for demonstration unit; commercial design uncertified |
| Holtec International | SMR-300 (PWR) | Various international proposals | Pre-application; no design certification |
| **NuScale** | **NPM (passive PWR)** | **Romania, TVA** | **Design Certification (Jan 2023) + Standard Design Approval (May 2025)** |

TerraPower's Natrium design — backed by Bill Gates and built around a sodium-cooled fast reactor with integrated molten-salt thermal storage — has attracted serious capital and government attention, with its first plant breaking ground near Kemmerer, Wyoming. But the NRC has not certified the Natrium design. X-energy's Xe-100, a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor, received a $1.2 billion ARDP award from the Department of Energy and counts Dow Chemical among its prospective industrial customers, but it too operates without a complete NRC design certification. Kairos Power obtained an NRC construction permit for its Hermes demonstration unit in Oak Ridge, Tennessee — a meaningful milestone — but a commercial-scale design certification remains years away. Holtec's SMR-300, despite an aggressive international marketing posture, has not progressed through the formal certification pipeline.

For a U.S. data-center operator, an industrial customer, or a regulated utility seeking a Combined License Application on any competitive commercial timeline through the late 2020s, there is, as of May 2026, no licensed alternative to NuScale's NPM in the U.S. market. That is a genuine moat, constructed over fifteen years and at a cost exceeding $600 million in Fluor equity alone.

## The International Competitive Field

The global picture is more complicated. The United Kingdom's Rolls-Royce SMR program — targeting a 470 MWe-per-unit pressurized light water reactor, roughly six times the output of a single NuScale module — has received UK government financial backing and is pursuing Generic Design Assessment through the Office for Nuclear Regulation. Rolls-Royce has framed its program around industrial-scale factory fabrication and UK domestic energy security; potential deployment timelines run to the early 2030s, broadly overlapping with NuScale's Romania and TVA ambitions. Its larger per-unit output changes the project economics fundamentally relative to NuScale's modular incremental model, creating a different value proposition for utilities with large, contiguous power needs.

Two programs have already crossed the finish line that NuScale is still approaching.
