China's HTR-PM at Shidaowan, a high-temperature gas-cooled pebble-bed reactor developed by Tsinghua University and CNNC, achieved commercial operation in 2023 — making it the world's first operational SMR of its type at commercial scale, though its 200 MWe output and state-directed deployment context make direct Western market comparison difficult. Russia's RITM-200 reactors, deployed on nuclear-powered icebreakers and in the Arctic floating power station at Pevek, represent a different competitive vector: Russian state nuclear export programs through Rosatom have signed agreements across Africa, Asia, and Eastern Europe, though Western sanctions have severely curtailed Rosatom's market access in European and NATO-aligned nations, benefiting NuScale in Romania specifically.

## The Cost-Per-MWh Problem

None of the regulatory advantages matter if NuScale cannot deliver power at a price customers will pay. The UAMPS Carbon Free Power Project collapse in November 2023 was, at its core, a cost-per-MWh failure, and understanding its structural drivers is essential to evaluating whether the Romania and TVA programs can succeed where Idaho failed.

When NuScale first proposed the UAMPS project, projected costs pointed toward a levelized cost of electricity below $60 per megawatt-hour. By January 2023, that figure had risen to approximately $89 per megawatt-hour for a scaled-back 462 MWe six-module plant, against an estimated cost that had ballooned from $3.6 billion in 2020 to $9.3 billion. The contemporaneous U.S. natural gas combined-cycle benchmark sat between $40 and $60 per MWh depending on prevailing Henry Hub prices and carbon cost assumptions. The arithmetic was brutal and public.

Three structural problems compounded each other at UAMPS. First, the Idaho National Laboratory site was a first-of-a-kind plant, meaning all development, regulatory, and construction costs landed entirely on a single 12-module project with no replication benefit. Second, the subscriber pool of municipal utilities was too small and too risk-averse to absorb escalating unit costs as participants withdrew. Third, the project occurred before the AI-driven demand surge transformed the economics of 24/7 baseload power, meaning the cost per MWh had to compete against cheap wholesale grid power rather than against the premium that data-center operators are demonstrably willing to pay for carbon-free firm capacity.

The Romania and TVA programs address the first and second problems. RoPower's Doicești site is a brownfield conversion of a former coal plant, reducing greenfield civil construction costs and utilizing existing grid interconnection infrastructure. The ENTRA1/TVA framework, if it proceeds to binding agreements, would spread first-of-a-kind costs across a multi-unit, multi-site deployment with the volume economics that UAMPS never achieved.

## The Doosan Manufacturing Thesis

The most concrete evidence of NRC moat translating into commercial readiness is Doosan Enerbility's fabrication of long-lead components for twelve NuScale Power Modules. Doosan — South Korea's premier heavy industrial manufacturer — began forging pressure vessels and reactor internals under a manufacturing preparedness agreement that predates any binding customer FID. That decision represents a commercial judgment by an experienced industrial partner that NuScale's design is stable enough to commit capital against before orders are confirmed.

The honest qualification is that Doosan's work remains in the first-of-a-kind cost category. The manufacturing learning curve that drives nth-of-a-kind cost reduction in factory production — the basis of NuScale's original modular thesis — requires serial production volumes that do not yet exist. Romania would be module sets one through six; early TVA units would follow. True factory-scale cost reduction requires dozens of modules across multiple sites. The gap between where NuScale is today and where its cost model optimizes is likely a decade of production volume.

## The AI Data-Center Moat

The AI/data-center opportunity represents perhaps the most important near-term competitive differentiator NuScale possesses, and it flows directly from NRC certification. A hyperscale operator building a data center campus requiring several hundred megawatts of 24/7 carbon-free power cannot simply substitute a competing SMR technology — any U.S. nuclear plant, regardless of design, requires an NRC Combined License. For TerraPower, X-energy, or Kairos to serve that same customer on a competitive timeline, they would need to complete design certification, prepare a COLA, and navigate a multi-year NRC review — a process that realistically extends past 2030 even under optimistic assumptions.

NuScale's SDA allows a U.S. data-center customer or its utility counterpart to reference the approved design immediately in a COLA filing, compressing the front-end regulatory timeline in a way no competitor can currently match. Standard Power's engagement and the advanced-dialogue status reported in Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 earnings calls suggest the company is actively pursuing this advantage. In a market where hyperscalers are signing long-duration power purchase agreements at premium prices to secure firm carbon-free capacity, the ability to credibly offer a licensed, financeable SMR on a 2030-era timeline may be worth more commercially than any marginal cost-per-MWh advantage a competing design might eventually achieve.

The risk is that the AI demand wave creates enough urgency to accelerate competing regulatory programs, or that gas with carbon capture or long-duration battery storage fills the gap before NuScale can execute. But as of May 2026, the queue is short and NuScale holds the only tickets.

chapters.title: News Catalysts: Key Events 2022-2026 and Forward Triggers Through 2028
chapters.body:
## The Public-Market Arc: SPAC Listing to Crisis, May 2022–November 2023

NuScale Power arrived on the New York Stock Exchange on May 2, 2022, through its merger with Spring Valley Acquisition Corp, raising approximately $380 million in gross proceeds and listing under the ticker SMR at what would prove to be a fleeting moment of euphoria. The SPAC era was already crumbling around it — but NuScale carried a credential no other SMR developer could match: the world's first small modular reactor to complete a full Nuclear Regulatory Commission design review, a Standard Design Approval that had cost fifteen years and over $600 million in Fluor Corporation equity to obtain. The stock climbed into the high teens in the months following the listing, buoyed by a macro energy anxiety sharpened by Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the European scramble for non-Russian baseload alternatives.

The first major sentiment shock arrived not with a dramatic announcement but with a cost disclosure. In January 2023, NuScale's lead customer, the Utah Associated Municipal Power Systems, revealed that the projected all-in cost of the Carbon Free Power Project at Idaho National Laboratory had ballooned to approximately $9.3 billion for a 462 MWe plant — more than double the $3.6 billion originally projected for 720 MWe in 2020. The implied levelized cost had risen toward $90 per megawatt-hour against a natural gas generation backdrop at roughly $40-50/MWh. UAMPS member utilities began withdrawing. NuScale's share price, which had briefly traded in the low $20s on the announcement of the NRC's 50 MWe standard design certification in January 2023, reversed sharply.

The formal death of UAMPS came in November 2023. NuScale cancelled the Carbon Free Power Project, laid off 154 employees representing 28 percent of its workforce, and accepted what amounted to a public verdict that first-of-a-kind nuclear construction economics had not yet been solved. The stock fell into the single digits, touching a 52-week low of $8.85 in the months that followed. The bear thesis had been vindicated, at least on the U.S. greenfield deployment model.

## Recovery Architecture: NRC Re-Certification and the ENTRA1 Pivot, 2024–2025

The company that emerged from the UAMPS wreckage rebuilt around a different commercial structure. NuScale's original ENTRA1 partnership, formalized in 2022 with the Habboush Group as principal backer, took on greater strategic weight as the company sought a commercialization vehicle that did not depend on NuScale itself absorbing project development risk. ENTRA1 held global exclusive commercialization rights to NuScale's technology, a structure that separated the licensing and engineering entity from the capital-intensive development function.

Two regulatory milestones anchored the recovery narrative. In May 2025, the NRC issued its Standard Design Approval for the uprated 77 MWe per-module design — ahead of schedule — making NuScale the first and only company to hold two separate NRC design approvals for an SMR. The achievement was operationally significant: the 77 MWe SDA superseded the original 50 MWe certification and applied directly to the VOYGR-4 and VOYGR-6 plant configurations being pursued in Romania and Tennessee. Customers could now reference the approved design in Combined License Applications without restarting the full review cycle.

The stock's recovery from sub-$9 to a 52-week high of $57.42 — a move of more than 500 percent — tracked this regulatory re-rating alongside a macro shift in the energy narrative. The AI infrastructure buildout, which had accelerated through 2024 and 2025 as hyperscalers signed unprecedented power purchase agreements, created a demand category that the UAMPS cost debate had not contemplated: operators willing to pay premium prices for 24/7 carbon-free power at gigawatt scale, independent of the grid. NuScale reported in its Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 earnings calls that it was in advanced dialogue with multiple data-center and AI infrastructure customers — though no binding term sheet had been signed as of the frozen snapshot date.

## The $750 Million Raise and the TVA Framework, Q4 2025

The single largest capital event of the post-SPAC period arrived in Q4 2025, when NuScale executed a $750 million at-the-market equity raise at prices that management later characterized as opportunistic relative to the company's cash needs. The issuance of 39.3 million Class A shares at elevated prices brought year-end liquidity to approximately $1.3 billion with zero long-term debt — a balance sheet position that afforded the company an estimated multi-year runway without emergency dilution. The Q4 2025 raise coincided almost exactly with the announcement of the ENTRA1-TVA non-binding collaborative framework: an agreement for the deployment of up to six gigawatts of NuScale capacity across TVA's seven-state service territory, which management characterized as the largest nuclear deployment initiative in U.S. history.

The TVA announcement sent the stock to its 52-week high near $57. The subsequent retracement — back below $15 by late May 2026 — illustrated the market's increasingly precise reading of the gap between framework agreements and binding commercial contracts. A Q1 2026 revenue collapse to $0.6 million from $13.4 million in Q1 2025, caused by the completion of the major RoPower engineering contracts in late 2025, reminded investors that NuScale's income remains episodic and milestone-driven. Meanwhile, Fluor Corporation's systematic divestiture from approximately 55 percent ownership at SPAC close to roughly 7.8 percent by early 2026 removed the last structural institutional anchor — though it distributed NuScale equity more broadly across public-market holders.

## Forward Triggers Through 2028

| Catalyst | Estimated Window | Potential Stock Impact |
|---|---|---|
| Romania RoPower FID announcement | H2 2026 | Significant positive — first binding customer contract |
| TVA Combined License Application filing | 2026–2027 | Positive — converts framework to regulatory action |
| First AI/data-center binding term sheet | 2026 | High impact — new demand category validated |
| Second-country FID (Poland/Ghana/other) | 2027 | Incremental positive — pipeline depth confirmed |
| DOE loan guarantee or financing commitment | 2026–2027 | Re-rating catalyst — reduces project finance risk |

The most proximate scheduled event after the frozen snapshot date is the annual shareholder meeting on May 29, 2026, where management is expected to address the Q1 2026 revenue decline, the Romania FID timeline, and the AI data-center dialogue. Investors will scrutinize any updated language around binding versus non-binding status for both the TVA and Romania programs.

The risk calendar is equally dense. A Romania FID delay beyond the 2026 calendar year would signal that European permitting and financing timelines — not NuScale's technology — are the binding constraint, and would likely compress the stock toward its net cash value of roughly $2.50 per share on a fully diluted basis. TVA converting its non-binding agreement to a binding contract with a cost-escalation disclosure echoing UAMPS would be the most damaging single event possible. A competitive SMR receiving NRC certification — no other developer had reached that milestone as of the frozen snapshot date, but X-energy and Kairos Power were in active review — would erode the regulatory moat thesis. And should Fluor complete its remaining approximately 7.8 percent exit, the last institutional memory of NuScale's engineering lineage would depart the cap table entirely, leaving the company's market narrative entirely in the hands of retail and event-driven hedge fund holders whose time horizons align poorly with a multi-year construction cycle.

chapters.title: Intellectual Property and R&D: The NRC Certification as Regulatory IP and the Design Upgrade Pipeline
chapters.body:
## The Regulatory Moat: Two Approvals, Fifteen Years

In the lexicon of conventional technology companies, intellectual property means patents, trade secrets, and source code. At NuScale Power, the most consequential piece of IP is a document issued by the United States Nuclear Regulatory Commission — and the decade-and-a-half of iterative regulatory engagement required to produce it.

The NRC issued its Design Certification for NuScale's original 50 megawatt-electric NuScale Power Module in January 2023, making NuScale the first and, as of the frozen snapshot date, the only small modular reactor developer in American history to clear that threshold. Sixteen months later, in May 2025, the agency issued a Standard Design Approval for the uprated 77 MWe configuration ahead of schedule, the second such approval NuScale has received. Taken together, the two approvals represent a regulatory moat that no rival SMR developer — not TerraPower, not X-energy, not the Rolls-Royce consortium in the United Kingdom — has come close to replicating in the United States. The NRC's design review process routinely requires more than a decade and consumes hundreds of millions of dollars in engineering documentation, safety analysis, and structured regulatory dialogue. Fluor Corporation's cumulative equity investment of more than $600 million, augmented by hundreds of millions in Department of Energy cost-share awards, financed that journey. The result is not merely a license; it is a compressing barrier to entry.

The practical commercial significance is specific. A utility or industrial customer seeking to deploy NuScale technology — RoPower in Romania, Tennessee Valley Authority through ENTRA1 — can reference either approved design in a Combined License Application to the NRC without reopening the underlying safety basis. That reference mechanism converts NuScale's historic regulatory spending into a time-to-deployment advantage of years relative to any competitor starting from a blank-sheet design.

## The Architecture of Passive Safety

The technological foundation underlying those approvals is an integral pressurized water reactor design in which both the primary coolant loop and the steam generator are contained within a single reactor pressure vessel — eliminating external primary coolant piping, which is the dominant source of large-break loss-of-coolant accidents in conventional PWR designs. The NPM's safety case rests on natural circulation: in the absence of pump power, coolant convects upward through the reactor core and downward through the steam generator purely by buoyancy-driven flow, transferring decay heat without mechanical intervention. Emergency core cooling is gravity-fed from pools above the reactor. The entire module sits below grade in a shared water pool that provides passive heat removal for seventy-two hours without operator action, external power, or active injection.

These architectural choices are not incidental. They are the product of research that began at Oregon State University under Department of Energy funding in 2000 and that NuScale's co-founder Dr. José N. Reyes Jr. developed into a licensable design over the following decade. The core passive-safety innovations are protected by an extensive patent portfolio. Because the safety case was built from first principles around passive physics rather than retrofitted onto a conventional active-system design, NuScale has argued — and the NRC has validated — that the design can meet its safety objectives without the layers of backup systems that drive capital cost in conventional large nuclear plants.

## Test Infrastructure as Living R&D

Supporting and defending those regulatory approvals is an ongoing experimental program at two integral test facilities. The OSU-MASLWR facility at Oregon State University replicates the NPM's thermal-hydraulic behavior at reduced scale, allowing researchers to validate natural circulation models and safety analysis codes under controlled conditions. SIET S.p.A. in Piacenza, Italy, operates a complementary high-pressure integral test facility focused on European regulatory acceptance pathways relevant to the Romania program. Both installations serve a dual function: they generate the empirical data that underpins regulatory defense of existing design approvals, and they provide the experimental foundation for future design iterations.

NuScale's research and development expenditures have reflected the pivot from the 50 MWe design to the uprated 77 MWe configuration and, increasingly, toward future derivative designs. In the first quarter of 2026, the company reported R&D spending approximately $3.7 million above the comparable Q1 2025 period, directed primarily toward higher-output module development and validation activities associated with the VOYGR-6 plant configuration being engineered for RoPower. The longer-term R&D trajectory visible in annual disclosures shows R&D as a meaningful but declining share of total operating expenses as the base design matured — a pattern consistent with a company whose core design-phase spending is behind it and whose incremental R&D is focused on configuration extensions rather than fundamental architecture.

## The Design Upgrade Pipeline

| Configuration | Modules | Gross Output | Regulatory Status (as of 2026-05-23) |
|---|---|---|---|
| VOYGR-4 | 4 | 308 MWe | Covered by May 2025 SDA |
| VOYGR-6 | 6 | 462 MWe | Covered by May 2025 SDA |
| VOYGR-12 | 12 | 924 MWe | License extension pending |

The VOYGR-12 configuration — twelve modules at a single site producing 924 MWe — remains a planned licensing extension rather than a certified design. At that output level, a NuScale plant approaches the capacity of a mid-sized conventional pressurized water reactor while retaining the modular phasing flexibility that distinguishes the NPM approach. Licensing the 12-module configuration requires an incremental NRC review layered onto the existing SDA, a structurally simpler process than re-certifying from scratch.

NuScale has also pursued process-heat variants that would allow the NPM to deliver high-temperature steam to chemical, hydrogen production, and desalination facilities rather than — or in addition to — generating electricity. A completed feasibility study validated the NPM's thermal output profile for industrial co-generation. Whether higher-assay low-enriched uranium fuel compatibility will be incorporated into a future design iteration remains an open development pathway; HALEU would, in principle, allow higher burnup cycles or extended refueling intervals, but the fuel supply chain for HALEU is not commercially mature, and NuScale's current design is optimized for the standard LWR fuel assemblies that Framatome and domestic enrichers already produce. The Q1 2026 expansion of the NuScale-Framatome fuel partnership targeted near-term supply chain certainty for the Romania and TVA programs rather than next-generation fuel cycle advancement.

## Licensing as Commercialization

NuScale's revenue model converts its regulatory IP into cash through technology licensing agreements. The company does not build reactors; it licenses a certified design to customers who contract separately for engineering, procurement, and construction. Under the ENTRA1 structure, NuScale's exclusive global commercialization partner holds the deployment rights for most markets, with license fee income flowing back to NuScale as engineering milestones are reached. The Romania program has been the primary source of recognizable licensing revenue in FY2024 and FY2025, with RoPower's FEED-phase engineering payments comprising the bulk of the company's $31.5 million in FY2025 revenue.

That revenue figure is modest against a cost structure that burns through capital at rates justified only by the size of the eventual deployment opportunity. But the underlying logic is that the NRC design approvals — NuScale's two fifteen-year-in-the-making regulatory artifacts — are, like a pharmaceutical company's FDA approvals, the central assets. Every competitor who begins the NRC review process today starts a clock that will not stop until the mid-2030s at the earliest. NuScale's clock stopped in May 2025.

chapters.title: Risks: Six Threats to Commercial Viability from Cost Escalation to Competing Technologies
chapters.body:
## The Ghost of UAMPS: Cost Escalation Recurrence

The single most damaging event in NuScale's corporate history was not a failed engineering test or a regulatory setback — it was a spreadsheet. When the projected all-in cost for the Utah Associated Municipal Power Systems Carbon Free Power Project rose from $3.6 billion for 720 MWe in 2020 to $9.3 billion for 462 MWe by January 2023, the implied levelized cost of electricity exceeded $90 per megawatt-hour in a market awash with cheap natural gas and subsidized renewables. UAMPS member utilities walked. NuScale shed 154 employees — 28 percent of its workforce. The stock collapsed.

The structural forces that produced that cost spiral have not been fully resolved. First-of-a-kind civil construction carries an inherent premium: every concrete pour, every equipment interface, every safety classification judgment is being made for the first time, generating rework and contingency that serial production eventually eliminates but that the inaugural plant must absorb. For Romania's Doicești site, NuScale and Nuclearelectrica completed a Phase 2 Front-End Engineering and Design study in 2025, but a FEED study is an estimate with confidence intervals, not a fixed-price commitment. Labor market conditions in Romanian civil construction and the pricing of specialized nuclear-grade steel and instrumentation from South Korean manufacturers like [Doosan Enerbility](https://www.nuscalepower.com/investors) remain subject to commodity cycle and exchange-rate volatility that no FEED study can fully insulate. The UAMPS project began with optimistic estimates and revised them upward three times in four years. Romania's Final Investment Decision, targeted for 2026, will need to price in contingency reserves that UAMPS demonstrably underweighted. If it does not, the same escalation dynamic that destroyed UAMPS could surface by 2027-2028 when first concrete is poured at Doicești.

For TVA, the geometry is different but the exposure is real. The non-binding six-gigawatt collaborative agreement signed in late 2025 spreads first-of-a-kind costs across a much larger base — in theory, the learning-curve economics that justify the program's scale. But "in theory" is carrying significant weight. Until TVA files site-specific Combined License Applications and commits to a fixed-price EPC structure, the program's cost envelope remains aspirational.

## ENTRA1 Concentration and the Habboush Group Dependency

NuScale's commercialization strategy outside its direct licensing relationships rests almost entirely on a single counterparty. ENTRA1 Energy, whose principals include members of the Habboush Group, holds exclusive global commercialization rights to NuScale's technology — a structure that generates both strategic leverage and concentrated risk. The TVA six-gigawatt program, the largest nuclear deployment initiative in U.S. history by management's own characterization, flows through ENTRA1, not directly between NuScale and TVA.

This creates a layered dependency that investors should examine carefully. If ENTRA1 proves unable to close binding contracts with sufficient speed, if its financing capacity is inadequate to backstop EPC cost guarantees, or if the Habboush Group principals encounter financial or reputational difficulties, NuScale has no independent commercial channel to substitute for ENTRA1's role in the TVA program. The company's [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001822966/000182296626000018/smr-20251231.htm) identified this concentration explicitly as a material risk. The $507.4 million Milestone Contribution 1 recognition in FY2025 G&A reflects how deeply the ENTRA1 partnership is embedded in NuScale's financial architecture — but milestone accounting is not the same as executed commercial commitments, and the non-cash nature of much of that recognition underscores how contingent the economics remain.

## Regulatory Latency Below the Design Approval

NuScale secured its first NRC design certification in January 2023 for the 50 MWe NPM and its second Standard Design Approval — for the uprated 77 MWe configuration — in May 2025. These achievements represent genuine regulatory moats: no other U.S. SMR developer has completed either process. However, they do not clear the regulatory path for any specific power plant. A Combined License Application for TVA or a U.S. data-center operator requires site-specific environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act, site-specific safety analysis to supplement the reference design, local and state permitting, and NRC staff review of the combined application — a process that has historically consumed three to five years for even well-prepared applicants. Any shift in NRC staffing priorities, policy interpretation on passive safety system review, or legal challenge to NEPA findings could introduce delays that compress the commercial window further.

Romania presents a partially different regulatory profile: Nuclearelectrica operates under Romanian and Euratom nuclear law, and the regulatory pathway is coordinated with Romanian nuclear authority CNCAN rather than the NRC. But the FEED study completion and FID commitment do not in themselves constitute a regulatory approval to construct or operate; that process remains parallel and could develop its own latency independent of project financing readiness.

## Competitive Displacement Before Contract Closure

NuScale's central competitive claim — that it is America's only NRC-certified SMR developer — is correct but time-bounded. The relevant competitive threat is not another U.S. developer achieving equivalent certification before NuScale closes commercial contracts; it is whether international programs achieve commercial operation first, eroding NuScale's first-mover premium and demonstrating to data-center and utility customers that an alternative path exists.

Rolls-Royce's UK SMR program, targeting 470 MWe per plant, received Generic Design Assessment progress from the UK's Office for Nuclear Regulation through 2024 and is pursuing British government support for a first deployment later this decade. If Rolls-Royce achieves commercial operation before NuScale's first plant enters service — or even before NuScale closes a binding U.S. contract — the claim that NuScale uniquely occupies the proven-SMR tier weakens. Chinese high-temperature gas-cooled reactor derivatives operating in demonstration mode provide a parallel competitive signal. AI hyperscalers evaluating 24/7 carbon-free baseload options are commercially agnostic: if a foreign-built SMR achieves commercial operation and can be deployed on contracted timelines shorter than NuScale's, project finance and customer preference may shift.

## Balance Sheet Endurance and Dilution Exposure

NuScale's capital structure is, by the standards of the pre-revenue nuclear development sector, unusually strong. Zero long-term debt, $1.3 billion in cash and short-term investments at year-end 2025, and approximately $1.0 billion remaining at the close of Q1 2026, after the quarterly cash burn, provide a credible three-to-four-year operating runway at current spending levels. The $750 million ATM raise in Q4 2025, which issued 39.3 million Class A shares, demonstrated continued investor appetite even after the Q1 2026 revenue miss — full-quarter revenue of $0.6 million against $13.4 million in Q1 2025 was a severe sequential decline reflecting the completion of major Romania FEED engineering contracts.

The risk is not immediate insolvency but the compounding dilution that additional equity raises impose if commercial milestones slip. If Romania's FID slides from 2026 into 2027 or 2028 — plausible given FEED-to-FID transition complexity and Romanian state budget processes — NuScale will enter a third equity raise cycle with a share count already expanded by the Q4 2025 ATM program.

| Capital Event | Shares Issued | Proceeds | Cumulative Dilution Effect |
|---|---|---|---|

Each additional raise at prices below the 52-week high of $57.42 — shares traded near $12.29 as of late May 2026 — extracts substantial dilution from existing shareholders relative to the post-SPAC entry point.

## Key-Person Concentration in a Thirteen-Year CEO Tenure

John Hopkins has served as President and Chief Executive Officer since December 2012 — thirteen and a half years across the company's most consequential regulatory milestones, its deepest financial crisis, and its current rebuilding phase. His tenure encompasses both NRC design certifications, the ENTRA1 partnership formation, the UAMPS cancellation and workforce reduction, the $750 million ATM raise, and the ongoing Romania FEED program. That institutional continuity is an asset: Hopkins carries firsthand knowledge of NRC staff relationships accumulated over a decade of design review, the Habboush Group partnership dynamics that underpin ENTRA1's commercialization role, and the DOE cost-share history that shapes NuScale's government affairs posture.

It is also a concentration risk. Annual total compensation of approximately $3.43 million for FY2024, structured roughly 18 percent in base salary and 82 percent in equity and performance-based awards, aligns Hopkins's incentives with long-term share appreciation. However, the [DEF 14A proxy](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001822966&type=DEF+14A) filed for the 2025 annual meeting does not disclose a named internal successor, and the board's compensation committee has not publicly articulated a formal CEO succession framework. For a company whose commercial viability depends on closing the first large-scale SMR deployment agreements in U.S. history — transactions that hinge as much on relationship continuity and regulatory credibility as on technical merit — the departure of a thirteen-year CEO before binding contracts are executed would constitute a materially disruptive event that the current governance structure appears insufficiently prepared to absorb.

chapters.title: Outlook: The 2026-2030 Horizon — FID, First Power, and the Trillion-Dollar SMR Market
chapters.body:
## Three Scenarios for a Defining Decade

The five years beginning in 2026 represent the period in which NuScale Power will either validate its fifteen-year regulatory investment or find itself stranded as a certification artifact in a market that outpaced it. Three plausible futures bracket the range of outcomes, and the distance between them turns almost entirely on two variables: whether Romania achieves a Final Investment Decision in 2026, and whether Tennessee Valley Authority converts its non-binding framework into a combined license application before the end of the decade.

In the **base case**, Romania's RoPower project reaches FID by late 2026, with SN Nuclearelectrica drawing on EU Just Transition Fund financing, a Romanian sovereign credit backstop, and committed equipment orders from Doosan Enerbility — whose ongoing fabrication of long-lead components for twelve NuScale Power Modules already constitutes the most advanced manufacturing activity in the program. TVA executes a binding collaborative agreement by 2027 covering initial site selection and engineering work, stopping short of a full EPC contract but sufficient to trigger combined license application filing at the NRC. First module operations at Doicești arrive by approximately 2031, consistent with the FEED study's indicative schedule, and NuScale begins recognizing capacity-payment or power-purchase revenue for the first time in its history. The share price, in this scenario, re-rates from its current trough toward a valuation that begins to discount commercial-stage cash flows rather than pure option value.

In the **bull case**, Romania FID and TVA's binding Collaborative License Agreement arrive simultaneously in 2026 or early 2027, joined by the first signed power purchase agreement with an AI data-center operator — the category of customer whose unhedged appetite for 24/7 carbon-free baseload has become NuScale management's most-cited commercial rationale. Multiple revenue streams mature before 2030: the Romania technology license generates staged payments through construction, TVA's program enters engineering procurement, and a data-center PPA provides contracted forward revenue. NuScale's quarterly revenue recovers from the $0.6 million reported in Q1 2026 toward double digits per quarter by 2028, substantially reducing the cash burn that has defined every year since the company's founding.

In the **bear case**, Romania's FID slips to 2028 under the weight of Romanian institutional financing gaps, EU regulatory sequencing, and Nuclearelectrica's limited balance sheet capacity — a utility that has been the primary vehicle for Romania's two operating CANDU reactors but has never financed a project of this capital magnitude. TVA remains non-binding through 2027 and into 2028, its six-state service territory absorbing cheaper renewable additions that reduce the urgency of nuclear baseload procurement. NuScale, burning approximately $30 to $60 million per quarter in cash operating expenses against sub-$10 million quarterly revenues, executes another equity raise in 2027 — likely at a share price materially below the current $12.29, given investor fatigue with repeated timeline extensions. The $1.3 billion cash position reported at year-end 2025 would contract to approximately $700 million to $900 million by that point, still solvent but with the runway narrative no longer as comfortable.

## The Macroeconomic Tailwind NuScale Did Not Have in 2023

The macro environment that surrounded the UAMPS cancellation in November 2023 — cheap natural gas, abundant renewable capacity additions, and an electricity market that discounted reliability premiums — has shifted materially. U.S. data center electricity consumption is projected to reach 35 to 50 gigawatts of incremental demand by 2030, according to multiple grid operator forecasts, with hyperscale operators increasingly unable to meet corporate clean-energy commitments using intermittent solar or wind. The structural problem is chronological: a data center running graphics processing units for large language model inference requires power every hour of every day; a solar farm in the mid-Atlantic delivers power perhaps 25 percent of the time.

The Inflation Reduction Act's nuclear production tax credit — $15 per megawatt-hour for qualifying advanced nuclear plants — applies to SMR technology and would meaningfully compress the all-in cost of power from a VOYGR-6 plant. At a projected levelized cost in the $70 to $100 per megawatt-hour range for first-of-a-kind NuScale plants, the PTC alone represents a 15 to 21 percent reduction in effective delivered cost to the offtaker. The current administration's explicit support for nuclear energy, combined with bipartisan backing for NRC reform legislation and potential fee reduction for advanced reactor licensing, creates a regulatory tail wind that was absent during the UAMPS era.

## Romania: Political Motivation Against Institutional Friction

Romania's European Union membership and its formal commitment to carbon neutrality by 2050 create genuine political motivation for the Doicești project to proceed. The conversion of a former coal plant site directly addresses EU Just Transition Fund eligibility criteria, and Romanian officials have framed the RoPower project as a cornerstone of national energy independence following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The Phase 2 FEED study completion and Nuclearelectrica shareholder approval to advance represent material progress that distinguishes this program from its counterparts in Poland, Ghana, and other pipeline markets.

The execution risk, however, is institutional rather than political. Nuclearelectrica has never led a greenfield nuclear construction project; Romania's development bank and sovereign credit structures are not configured to backstop a $6 to $7 billion first-of-a-kind nuclear plant without substantial EU co-financing. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the U.S. Export-Import Bank have both engaged with the project at various stages, but committed project finance with locked interest rates and currency protections had not been announced as of the frozen snapshot date. If EU regulatory approvals for state aid and environmental impact assessment stretch through 2026, the FID window narrows to late 2026 at best.

## TVA and the Factory-Fabrication Thesis

The six-gigawatt TVA framework is the single most consequential variable for NuScale's long-term economics, for reasons that extend well beyond the revenue it would generate. Six gigawatts of NuScale capacity implies approximately 78 NuScale Power Modules distributed across roughly thirteen VOYGR-6 plants. At that volume, the learning-curve and series-manufacturing arguments that underpin the factory-fabrication thesis become empirically testable rather than theoretical. Doosan Enerbility's assembly line, Framatome's fuel delivery infrastructure, and the domestic supply chain being built around the Charlotte and Rockville engineering offices could all transition from custom-project to production-rate economics.

The financial implication is significant. A single VOYGR-6 plant at $6 to $7 billion in total project cost, with NuScale earning a technology license royalty and engineering services margin estimated conservatively at 8 to 12 percent of project cost, would contribute approximately $480 million to $840 million in NuScale revenue spread across a five-to-seven-year construction period — roughly $70 million to $170 million annually per plant under construction. At a steady-state cash operating burn of $120 to $240 million per year, NuScale would require two to three plants simultaneously in active construction to approach operating cash flow breakeven. That threshold implies three to four binding EPC contracts — a milestone that would require Romania plus at least two TVA sites in concurrent construction, a scenario that falls somewhere between the base case and the bull case.

## The Strategic Endgame

The question the dossier ultimately poses is whether NuScale's first-mover regulatory advantage — the only NRC-certified SMR design on the planet, a certification that took a decade and cost hundreds of millions — constitutes a durable commercial moat or a depreciating asset. The $4.5 billion market capitalization at late May 2026 prices the company as something between a technology licensing platform and a pre-revenue nuclear utility. Neither framing is quite right.

If Romania reaches FID and TVA converts, NuScale becomes the operating company that proves the SMR cost thesis and owns the de-facto reference design for a global wave of deployments. If those milestones slip past 2028, the more likely outcome is that a better-capitalized strategic acquirer — a Doosan, a Framatome parent ORANO, a South Korean utility, or a U.S. defense contractor with nuclear ambitions — concludes that NuScale's certification and engineering IP is worth more to its balance sheet than NuScale's current shareholders are being compensated for. John Hopkins has spent thirteen years ensuring the first outcome remains possible. The next eighteen months will determine which path the company is actually on.

## Glossary

**ATM** — At-the-market equity program; continuous share issuance into open-market trading at prevailing prices, used by NuScale to raise $750 million in Q4 2025.

**CFPP** — Carbon Free Power Project; the UAMPS-led Idaho National Laboratory deployment program cancelled in November 2023 after projected costs reached $9.3 billion.

**FEED** — Front-End Engineering and Design; detailed pre-construction engineering work used to establish project cost and schedule baselines before a Final Investment Decision.

**FID** — Final Investment Decision; the binding commitment by project sponsors and financiers to proceed to construction, triggering EPC contract execution.

**NDA** — Nuclear Design Approval; a regulatory milestone in certain non-U.S. jurisdictions (notably the UK Generic Design Assessment process) confirming design acceptability.

**NPM** — NuScale Power Module; NuScale's proprietary integral pressurized light water reactor unit, rated at 77 MWe / 250 MWt in its current uprated configuration.

**NRC** — Nuclear Regulatory Commission; the independent U.S. federal agency responsible for licensing and regulating commercial nuclear reactors and fuel cycle facilities.

**SDA** — Standard Design Approval; an NRC approval confirming that a reactor design meets regulatory requirements, allowing customers to reference the approved design in Combined License Applications without repeating the full design review. NuScale received its SDA for the 77 MWe NPM in May 2025.

**SPAC** — Special Purpose Acquisition Company; a blank-check shell company that merges with an operating business to effect a public listing; NuScale merged with Spring Valley Acquisition Corp in May 2022.

**VOYGR** — NuScale's commercial plant configuration family, offered in VOYGR-4 (308 MWe), VOYGR-6 (462 MWe), and VOYGR-12 (924 MWe) increments using standardised NPM arrays.

financials.key_finding: NuScale Power is a pre-commercial operating company whose financial profile is defined entirely by cash consumption, capital structure management, and milestone-contingent non-cash accounting items rather than by conventional revenue or earnings metrics. Full-year 2025 revenue was $31.5 million, down from $37.0 million in FY2024, with essentially all income derived from engineering services fees, technology licensing agreements (primarily the RoPower technology license), and DOE cost-sharing reimbursements. The company has never generated revenue from power sales or capacity payments. Cost of sales reached $20.0 million in FY2025 against $4.9 million in FY2024, driven by expanded engineering deliverables for the Romania FEED program. The most anomalous line in the P&L is G&A expense of $609.8 million in FY2025 versus $75.9 million in FY2024 — an increase attributable to recognition of $507.4 million in non-cash or milestone-contingent Milestone Contribution 1 under the Partnership Milestone Agreement with ENTRA1 Energy, which inflated the GAAP loss without representing operating cash outflow at equivalent magnitude. Net loss for FY2025 was approximately $355.8 million. Q1 2026 revenue collapsed to $0.6 million versus $13.4 million in Q1 2025, a 95.5 percent sequential year-over-year decline caused by the completion of major engineering contracts in late 2025. The capital structure is unusually clean for a development-stage company: zero long-term debt as of year-end 2025, and $1.3 billion in cash, equivalents, and short-term investments following a $750 million at-the-market equity raise in Q4 2025 that sold 39.3 million Class A shares. Market capitalization as of late May 2026 was approximately $4.5 billion on a share price near $12.29, down sharply from the 52-week high of $57.42, reflecting investor reassessment of commercialization timelines after the Q1 2026 revenue miss. Investment income of $25.3 million in FY2025 (up from $8.4 million in FY2024) reflects the yield on the large cash balance. Forward financial inflection depends entirely on whether Romania achieves FID in 2026 and whether TVA or another U.S. customer executes a binding EPC contract, neither of which was confirmed as of the frozen snapshot date.
structural_observations: Revenue is entirely pre-commercial and episodic: FY2025 revenue of $31.5 million was driven by the RoPower Romania technology license fee and related engineering services; Q1 2026 revenue of $0.6 million confirmed the lumpy, milestone-driven nature of the income stream with no contracted recurring base.

Fiscal year ends December 31; NuScale reports on a quarterly cadence with SEC filings on Form 10-K, 10-Q, and 8-K; the company has been a public reporting company since completing the Spring Valley SPAC merger in May 2022.

GAAP G&A expense is severely distorted by non-cash partnership milestone accounting: the $609.8 million FY2025 G&A figure includes $507.4 million in Milestone Contribution 1 recognition under the ENTRA1 Partnership Milestone Agreement, making period-to-period expense comparisons meaningless without stripping this item; cash G&A was far lower.

Capital structure is development-stage clean: zero long-term debt, $1.3 billion liquidity at year-end 2025, and $1.0 billion at end of Q1 2026; the company has relied on equity financing (SPAC proceeds in 2022, ATM programs in 2024 and 2025) and no interest-bearing debt obligations; this structure is sustainable only as long as investors accept pre-revenue narrative.

Fluor Corporation's systematic divestiture from approximately 55 percent ownership at SPAC close in 2022 to approximately 7.8 percent by April 2026 removed a strategic anchor shareholder and increased float, contributing to share price volatility; the 52-week trading range of $8.85 to $57.42 as of late May 2026 reflects extreme sentiment swings tied to commercialization news.

Closest comparable peers are pre-revenue nuclear technology developers including X-energy, TerraPower, and Kairos Power (all private), and the broader clean-energy SPAC cohort that went public in 2021-2022; no direct public-market SMR comparables exist with equivalent regulatory progress, making conventional P/E or EV/EBITDA multiples inapplicable — investors price NuScale on option value and timeline probability.

Forward financial inflection requires at least one binding commercial contract: the Romania RoPower project at approximately $6-7 billion total estimated cost and the ENTRA1/TVA 6-gigawatt program represent the only near-term candidates; without a Final Investment Decision with committed financing, NuScale will continue burning $30-60 million per quarter in cash operating expenses while recognizing sub-$10 million quarterly revenues.

leadership.key_finding: NuScale's executive leadership is anchored by a long-tenured CEO who has survived the company's two existential crises and remains its public face, alongside a CFO installed during the post-UAMPS restructuring and a newly appointed non-executive chairman who separates the board chair and CEO roles. John L. Hopkins has served as President and CEO since December 2012, making him one of the longest-serving small modular reactor executives globally. His reported FY2024 total compensation of approximately $3.43 million — weighted approximately 82 percent toward equity and performance-based awards — aligns his incentive structure tightly with stock price recovery and commercialization milestones. Hopkins has navigated the company through the 2011 Fluor rescue, the 2022 SPAC listing, the 2023 UAMPS cancellation and associated 28-percent workforce reduction, and the subsequent 2025 capital raise of $750 million. His public communications emphasize NuScale's regulatory primacy and the AI-power demand thesis as the primary commercial catalyst. CFO Ramsey Hamady joined in August 2023, replacing the prior CFO during the post-UAMPS recovery period. Hamady brings a background from high-growth and capital markets-intensive companies including Equify Financial and Western Magnesium Corporation, with 26 years of experience in private and public SEC-reporting organizations. His arrival signaled a shift toward capital markets credibility and balance sheet management as priorities. Non-Executive Chairman Alan Boeckmann assumed the chairmanship effective January 15, 2025, in a leadership transition that separated the CEO and board chair roles — a governance improvement that proxy advisory firms and institutional investors generally view favorably. The board of nine includes directors with nuclear, defense, engineering, and financial backgrounds: Alan Boeckmann, Bum-Jin Chung, Shinji Fujino, Stuart Harshaw, John L. Hopkins, Dale Klein (former NRC chairman), Kent Kresa, Diana Walters, and Kimberly Warnica. No private equity sponsor holds a controlling board seat; Fluor's reduction to 7.8 percent ownership by April 2026 effectively ended its board influence.
research_notes_for_writer: Verify whether Dale Klein's NRC chairmanship background (he served as NRC chairman from 2006-2009) creates any actual regulatory advantage or is primarily cosmetic governance optics — the chapter should not overstate the practical benefit of board-level NRC alumni presence.

The ENTRA1 Energy partnership is described as providing Habboush Group as a principal; the identity, capital base, and track record of the Habboush Group and whether ENTRA1 has the financial capacity to close FIDs on multi-billion-dollar nuclear projects deserves deep scrutiny and should be explored in the leadership chapter through proxy filings and any public disclosure.

Confirm whether CFO Ramsey Hamady executed the $750 million ATM in Q4 2025 and whether his prior experience at smaller companies adequately prepared NuScale for the complexity of this-scale capital markets execution — the CFO's role in the TVA and Romania FID processes is a forward question worth examining.

Hopkins's compensation structure relative to commercialization milestone achievement should be extracted from the DEF 14A proxy filings; specifically whether executive compensation vesting is tied to Romania FID, TVA combined license application filing, or other hard milestones vs. time-based vesting alone.

Bum-Jin Chung and Shinji Fujino are likely nominees of Asian strategic partners or investors — research their affiliations (Doosan Enerbility, Japanese utilities, or similar nuclear supply chain stakeholders) to determine whether their board seats represent governance of key commercial relationships.

Fluor's exit from 55 percent to 7.8 percent ownership over 2022-2026 warrants a paragraph exploring whether this divestiture was a planned return of capital to Fluor shareholders or reflected a loss of strategic confidence in NuScale's commercialization trajectory — Fluor's public statements on the share sales should be pulled from their 8-K filings.

The separation of CEO and Chairman roles in January 2025 was a governance improvement, but examine whether the board composition reflects sufficient independence given that ENTRA1 (the commercialization partner whose milestone payments dominate the P&L) is not represented on the board and its principal Habboush has no disclosed board role.
